title: Word "ROORKEE" is given to us. What is the probability
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: A word "ROORKEE" is given to us. What is the probability that same letters will always be together on making the words from the letters of the word taken all at a time ?
solution:
Concept: For a word with repeated letters, the number of distinct arrangements of all its letters equals n! divided by the factorial of each letter's repetition count. To force certain letters to always stay together, bundle each such repeated group into one single unit, arrange the reduced set of units, and take probability as (favourable arrangements) / (total arrangements).

Application

  1. "ROORKEE" has 7 letters: R, O, O, R, K, E, E — R repeats 2 times, O repeats 2 times, E repeats 2 times, and K occurs once.

  2. Total distinct arrangements of all 7 letters = 7! / (2! × 2! × 2!) = 5040 / 8 = 630.

  3. For the favourable case, bundle each repeated pair as one block — (RR), (OO), (EE) — together with K, giving 4 distinct units to arrange.

  4. Arrange these 4 units: 4! = 24 favourable arrangements (no extra internal arranging is needed inside a block since its two letters are identical).

  5. Probability = favourable / total = 24 / 630.

  6. Simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by 6: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 630 ÷ 6 = 105, giving 4/105.

The two fractions 24/630 and 4/105 are also numerically equal (both ≈ 0.0381), confirming the simplification is correct and no arrangement was double-counted, since dividing by 2!×2!×2! in step 2 already accounts for the identical letters inside each pair.

So the probability that the identical letters stay together is 24/630 = 4/105.

title: How many positive integers less than are such that the
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: How many positive integers less than 10,000 are such that the product of their digits is 210?
solution:
Answer: 54.

Prime factorization: 210 = 2 × 3 × 5 × 7. Digits must be between 1 and 9 (zero is not allowed because it would make the product 0), and we may use the digit 1 to fill extra positions.

  • Four-digit numbers: The primes can be placed as four separate digits giving {2, 3, 5, 7}, or combine 2 and 3 into 6 and use a 1 giving {1, 6, 5, 7}. Any other grouping of the primes produces a factor greater than 9 (for example 2×5 = 10), so these are the only two multisets. Each multiset has four distinct digits, so each yields 4! = 24 permutations, for 24 + 24 = 48 four-digit numbers.

  • Three-digit numbers: The only way to get three digits is to combine two primes into one digit and leave the other prime as separate digits; the only valid digit from combining two primes that stays ≤ 9 is 2×3 = 6, giving {6, 5, 7}. These are three distinct digits, so there are 3! = 6 such numbers.

  • One- and two-digit numbers: Impossible, because 210 cannot be represented as the product of one digit (≤9) or two digits (each ≤9).

Total count: 48 (four-digit) + 6 (three-digit) = 54.

title: Hall has gates. In how many ways, can man enter
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: A hall has 14 gates. In how many ways, can a man enter the hall through one gate and come out through a different gate?
solution:
Concept

When a task is carried out in stages performed one after another, the total number of ways is the product of the number of choices available at each stage — the fundamental counting principle. If both stages draw from the same pool of k distinct objects and the second stage may not repeat the object chosen at the first, then the first stage offers k choices and the second offers only k − 1, so the number of ordered pairs of distinct objects is k × (k − 1).

This count is exactly the number of ordered selections of 2 distinct objects out of k. Order is part of the arrangement, so a pair taken in one sequence is counted separately from the same pair taken in the opposite sequence.

Applying it here

  1. The pool here is the hall's 14 gates, and the man performs two ordered stages: he picks the gate he enters by, and then the gate he leaves by.

  2. Entry stage: any gate of the hall may be used, so there are 14 choices.

  3. Exit stage: the gate already used to enter is barred, so 13 of the 14 gates remain and there are 13 choices.

  4. By the counting principle the two stages multiply: 14 × 13 = 182 ways.

Cross-check

Count it the other way round as a check. Ignoring the restriction there are 14 × 14 = 196 ordered (entry gate, exit gate) pairs. Exactly 14 of these use the same gate twice, one for each gate, so the admissible count is 196 − 14 = 182, which matches the direct count.

In permutation notation the same figure is 14P2 = 14! / 12! = 14 × 13 = 182.

text: The number of ways to arrange 8 people in a circle such that two specific people are never adjacent is:
solution:
Concept: For n distinct people seated around a circular table, rotations of the same arrangement are treated as identical, so the number of distinct circular arrangements is (n − 1)! — fixing one person's seat removes the rotational symmetry, and the rest are arranged freely in the remaining seats. To count arrangements in which two specific people are never adjacent, use complementary counting: required arrangements = (arrangements with no restriction) − (arrangements in which the two are adjacent).

  1. Total circular arrangements of 8 people = (8 − 1)! = 7! = 5040.

  2. To count the arrangements in which the two specific people ARE adjacent, glue them into a single block. This leaves 7 units (the block plus the other 6 people) to arrange in a circle: (7 − 1)! = 6! = 720 ways.

  3. Within the block, the two people can be ordered in 2! = 2 ways, so the number of adjacent arrangements = 720 × 2 = 1440.

  4. Required (never-adjacent) arrangements = Total − Adjacent = 5040 − 1440 = 3600.

Cross-check: Fix one of the two specific people in a seat to remove rotational symmetry; the remaining 7 people then fill the other 7 seats in 7! = 5040 ways, matching the total above. Among these, the other specific person occupies one of the 2 seats adjacent to the fixed person in 2 ways, and the remaining 6 people fill the remaining 6 seats in 6! = 720 ways, giving 2 × 720 = 1440 adjacent arrangements — the same figure obtained by the block method, confirming the final count of 5040 − 1440 = 3600.

title: From character string of length the number of sub-strings of
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: From a character string of length m, the number of sub-strings of all lengths that can be formed are:
solution:
Concept: A substring of a string is any contiguous run of characters within it, and each occurrence of a substring is uniquely fixed by choosing a start position and an end position with start ≤ end (this counts substrings by position/occurrence, not distinct string values — repeated characters do not merge positions). So counting “all substrings of all lengths” is the same as counting how many valid (start, end) position pairs exist — which reduces to summing consecutive integers, the same triangular-number pattern used to count pairings among a set of positions.

  1. Number the character positions of the string 1 through m.

  2. A substring starting at position i can end at position i, i+1, …, or m — that gives (m − i + 1) valid substrings starting at position i.

  3. Summing this count over every starting position i = 1, 2, …, m gives: m + (m−1) + (m−2) + … + 1.

  4. This is the sum of the first m positive integers — an arithmetic series whose value is m(m+1)/2.

Cross-check: for m = 3 (string “abc”), the substrings are a, b, c (length 1), ab, bc (length 2), and abc (length 3) — 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 in total, and the formula gives 3(3+1)/2 = 6. The two match, confirming m(m+1)/2.

We need to find how many ways we can choose a pair of 2 people out of 8.

The formula for combinations is nCr = n! / (r! * (n - r)!).

The first person shakes hands with 7 others.

The second person shakes hands with 6 others (excluding the first).

The third person shakes hands with 5 others, and so on.

Total = 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 28.

subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: From a group of 7 men and 6 women, a committee of 5 persons with more males than females is to be formed. In how many ways can this be done?
solution:
Concept

A committee is an unordered selection, so each gender group is chosen with the combination nCr = n! / (r!(n−r)!). The condition "more males than females" in a 5-member committee means the number of men chosen must strictly exceed the number of women chosen. Enumerate every gender split that satisfies this, count each independently, then add (the splits are mutually exclusive).

Application

With 5 members and men > women, the only valid splits of (men, women) are (5, 0), (4, 1) and (3, 2). Count each from 7 men and 6 women:

  1. (5 men, 0 women): 7C5 × 6C0 = 21 × 1 = 21

  2. (4 men, 1 woman): 7C4 × 6C1 = 35 × 6 = 210

  3. (3 men, 2 women): 7C3 × 6C2 = 35 × 15 = 525

Total = 21 + 210 + 525 = 756.

Cross-check

The remaining splits (2 men, 3 women), (1 man, 4 women) and (0 men, 5 women) all have women ≥ men, so they are correctly excluded. Including every split of 5 from the 13 people would give 13C5 = 1287; our answer 756 is the strict-majority-male portion of that, which is consistent.

Restricting the cases this way changes the result.

title: There are persons in party. If each person shakes hands
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: There are 10 persons in a party. If each person shakes hands with every other person exactly once, the total number of handshakes is
solution:
To find the total number of handshakes when each person shakes hands with every other person exactly once, we use the combination formula.

Step 1: A handshake involves 2 people, so we need to find the number of ways to choose 2 people from 10.

Step 2: The combination formula is C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2, where n is the total number of people.

Step 3: Substitute n = 10: C(10,2) = 10×9/2 = 45.

Thus, the total number of handshakes is 45.

title: 4-digit number is to be formed using the digits such
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: A 4-digit number is to be formed using the digits 1,2,3,4,5,6 such that no digit repeats and the number is divisible by 3. How many such numbers can be formed?
solution:
Key idea: a number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. We choose 4 distinct digits from {1,2,3,4,5,6} whose sum is a multiple of 3, then count their permutations.

  • Residues modulo 3 for the digits: 1→1, 2→2, 3→0, 4→1, 5→2, 6→0. So residue groups are: residue 0: {3,6} (2 digits), residue 1: {1,4} (2 digits), residue 2: {2,5} (2 digits).

  • Let a,b,c be the numbers of chosen digits from residues 0,1,2 respectively. We need a+b+c=4 with each ≤2. The sum is divisible by 3 when b+2c ≡ 0 (mod 3). The valid distributions are (a,b,c) = (0,2,2) and (2,1,1).

  • Count the sets and permutations for each case:

    • (0,2,2): choose both digits from residue 1 (only one way) and both from residue 2 (only one way). This yields the single set {1,2,4,5}. Each set gives 4! = 24 permutations, so this case gives 24 numbers.

    • (2,1,1): choose both residue 0 digits (only one way), choose 1 of the 2 digits from residue 1 (2 choices) and 1 of the 2 digits from residue 2 (2 choices). That gives 1×2×2 = 4 distinct sets. Each set yields 4! = 24 permutations, so this case gives 4×24 = 96 numbers.

Total numbers = 24 + 96 = 120. Therefore the correct count is 120; the previously stated total of 216 was incorrect because the selection and permutation counts were not derived correctly.

title: In tournament teams play league matches. If each team plays
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: In a tournament 14 teams play league matches. If each team plays against every other team once only, then how many matches are played?
solution:
Concept

A single round-robin match is determined by an unordered pair of distinct teams. Reversing the two teams does not create a new match, so the number of matches among n teams is C(n, 2) = n(n − 1) / 2.

Equivalently, each successive team contributes one fewer new opponent, giving the sum (n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1.

Application

  1. Here n = 14.

  2. Substitute into the pair-count formula: C(14, 2) = 14 × 13 / 2.

  3. Compute the numerator: 14 × 13 = 182.

  4. Divide by 2: 182 / 2 = 91.

Cross-check

  1. Count only new opponents: the teams contribute 13, 12, 11, …, 1 new match in turn.

  2. The arithmetic-series sum is 13 × 14 / 2 = 91, which agrees with the combination count.

Result

Therefore, the league contains 91 matches.

text: 9 balls are to be placed in 9 boxes and 5 of the balls cannot fit into 3 small boxes. The number of ways of arranging one ball in each of the boxes is
solution:
We have 9 distinct balls and 9 boxes, with exactly one ball going into each box. Three of the boxes are 'small', and 5 of the 9 balls are too big to fit into any of these 3 small boxes.

Step 1 — Place the 5 large balls. These 5 balls can only go into the 9 - 3 = 6 boxes that are not small. The number of ways to arrange 5 distinct balls into 6 boxes (one per box) is the permutation P(6, 5) = 6!/(6-5)! = 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 = 720.

Step 2 — Place the remaining 4 balls. After placing the 5 large balls, 9 - 5 = 4 boxes remain empty and 4 balls remain. These 4 balls have no restriction, so they can be arranged in the 4 remaining boxes in 4! = 24 ways.

Step 3 — Combine. By the multiplication principle, the total number of arrangements is 720 x 24 = 17280.

Therefore, the number of ways of arranging one ball in each of the boxes is 17280.

title: The number of bit strings of length that contain either
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: The number of bit strings of length 10 that contain either five consecutive 0’s or five consecutive 1’s is
solution:
Concept

When a set is described by 'either A or B', its size is found by the Inclusion–Exclusion Principle: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. We add the two counts and subtract the overlap once, so strings satisfying both conditions are not counted twice.

Here A = bit strings of length 10 with at least five consecutive 0’s, and B = bit strings of length 10 with at least five consecutive 1’s.

Application

Count |A| (at least five consecutive 0’s) by where the first run of five 0’s begins:

  1. If the block of five 0’s starts at position 1, the remaining 5 bits are free: 2⁵ = 32 strings.

  2. If it starts at position 2, position 1 must be 1 (so the run is the first run of five), and the last 4 bits are free: 1·2⁴ = 16 strings.

  3. Starting at positions 3, 4, 5 and 6 each forces a 1 just before the block and leaves the rest free, giving 16 strings each.

  4. Total |A| = 32 + 16 + 16 + 16 + 16 + 16 = 112. By the 0↔ 1 symmetry, |B| = 112 as well.

  5. Overlap |A ∩ B|: a length‑10 string holding five consecutive 0’s and five consecutive 1’s must be exactly 0000011111 or 1111100000, so |A ∩ B| = 2.

  6. Apply inclusion–exclusion: |A ∪ B| = 112 + 112 − 2 = 222.

Cross-check

A direct enumeration over all 2¹⁰ = 1024 strings of length 10 yields exactly 222 strings meeting the condition, matching the inclusion–exclusion result.

optionFeedback.html: 64 equals 2⁶ and comes from a faulty block-placement count that treats the six possible starting positions of the five-symbol run as a single base-two exponent. That conflates positions with free bits and ignores the second symbol entirely.

112 reflects counting strings whose five-in-a-row are all the same single symbol, while treating that as the whole answer. The 'either … or' wording means the strings whose five-in-a-row are the OTHER symbol must also be included, so this stops short of the full set.

220 comes from over-correcting for the strings that satisfy both conditions: those few shared strings are taken out one time too many. Removing a shared group more than the single time the counting principle calls for pushes the total below the true value.

222 follows from adding the two single-symbol counts and removing their overlap exactly once: 112 + 112 − 2. The two strings that contain both runs are counted a single time, which is precisely what inclusion–exclusion requires.

title: If square matrix satisfies then the matrix, is
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Matrix and Vectors - Definition and Types
text: If a square matrix A satisfies AT A = I, then the matrix A is:
solution:
Concept: A real square matrix A is called an orthogonal matrix precisely when its transpose equals its inverse, i.e. AT A = A AT = I. This is one of several standard matrix-type definitions built from the transpose/conjugate-transpose relation: idempotent (A2 = A), symmetric (AT = A), orthogonal (AT A = I), and Hermitian (A* = A, using the conjugate transpose, for complex matrices).

Application: The question gives AT A = I. This is exactly the orthogonal-matrix condition above: it says AT is a left inverse of A. For a square matrix, a left inverse is automatically a two-sided inverse, so AT = A-1 — which is the defining property of an orthogonal matrix.

Cross-check: Testing AT A = I against each of the other named properties confirms none of them is what the condition actually states:

  • Idempotent (A2 = A) relates A to its own square, not to its transpose and the identity — a different equation, not implied by AT A = I in general.

  • Symmetric (AT = A) compares A directly with its own transpose; a matrix can satisfy AT A = I without AT equalling A — e.g. a 2D rotation matrix is orthogonal but not symmetric (unless the rotation angle is an integer multiple of pi).

  • Hermitian (A* = A) uses the conjugate transpose, a concept for complex-valued matrices; the given condition uses the plain (real) transpose, so it does not match the Hermitian definition.

So the condition AT A = I identifies A as an Orthogonal matrix.

optionFeedback.html: Idempotent matrices satisfy A2 = A -- applying the matrix twice has the same effect as applying it once, as with a projection onto a subspace. Every idempotent matrix other than the identity matrix is singular: it sends at least one nonzero vector to the zero vector, so it cannot be invertible.

A symmetric matrix satisfies AT = A -- it equals its own mirror image across the main diagonal. The 2D rotation matrix with entries cos(theta), -sin(theta), sin(theta), cos(theta) satisfies AT A = I for every angle theta, yet its transpose equals itself only when theta is an integer multiple of pi -- so most matrices with this invertibility-via-transpose property are not symmetric.

AT A = I is exactly the defining property of an orthogonal matrix: it says the transpose of A acts as A's inverse (AT = A-1), which is the standard definition of orthogonality for a real square matrix.

A Hermitian matrix satisfies A* = A using the conjugate transpose -- for a matrix of only real entries this reduces to the same requirement as AT = A, so Hermitian and symmetric coincide for real matrices. A 2D rotation matrix with entries cos(theta), -sin(theta), sin(theta), cos(theta) satisfies AT A = I for every angle theta, yet equals its own transpose only when theta is an integer multiple of pi -- so a real matrix can have its transpose serve as a two-sided inverse without being Hermitian.

  1. A is orthogonal, so by definition A·AT = I.

  2. Take the determinant of both sides: det(A·AT) = det(I).

  3. Use det(XY) = det(X)·det(Y) on the left and det(I) = 1 on the right: det(A)·det(AT) = 1.

  4. Since det(AT) = det(A) for any square matrix, substitute: det(A)2 = 1.

  5. Solve the equation det(A)2 = 1: det(A) = ±1.

Therefore the determinant of an orthogonal matrix of order n is ±1.

Cross-check

The result holds for both families of orthogonal matrices: a rotation matrix (e.g. the standard 2-D rotation matrix) is orthogonal with determinant cos2θ + sin2θ = 1, while a reflection matrix is orthogonal with determinant -1. Both satisfy det(A)2 = 1, confirming the value is always ±1 regardless of the order n.

title: Choose the statements which are correct always Real symmetric matrix’s
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text:
Choose the statements which are correct always
I) Real symmetric matrix’s eigenvalues are always real eigenvalues
II) For a non-square matrix, determinant is undefined
III) Singular matrix determinant is always 1
IV) Orthogonal matrices has determinant -1.
solution:
Answer: The statements "Real symmetric matrix’s eigenvalues are always real eigenvalues" and "For a non-square matrix, determinant is undefined" are correct; the other two statements are incorrect.

  • Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues: real symmetric matrices represent self-adjoint linear operators (with respect to the standard inner product), so all eigenvalues are real.

  • Determinant is undefined for non-square matrices: the determinant is defined only for square matrices, so it does not exist for non-square matrices.

Why the other statements are wrong:

  • The claim that a singular matrix has determinant 1 is false: a singular matrix is one with determinant 0.

  • The claim that orthogonal matrices have determinant -1 is false: an orthogonal matrix has determinant either +1 or -1, so it is not always -1.

Therefore, the correct combination is the two true statements listed above (real symmetric eigenvalues are real, and determinant is undefined for non-square matrices).

title: If the sum of diagonal elements of symmetric matrix is
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If the sum of diagonal elements of a 2×2 symmetric matrix is −8, then the maximum possible value of the determinant of the matrix is ________.
solution:
Concept: For a real 2×2 symmetric matrix A = [a b; b d], the determinant is |A| = ad − b2. Since b2 is never negative, the determinant can never exceed the product ad, and for two real numbers whose sum is fixed, their product is largest when the two numbers are equal to each other.

  1. Let the symmetric matrix be A = [a b; b d]. The given condition is the trace a + d = −8.

  2. The determinant of A is |A| = ad − b2.

  3. Because b2 ≥ 0 for every real b, |A| ≤ ad, with equality exactly when b = 0. So the largest possible determinant occurs at b = 0, and the problem reduces to maximizing ad subject to a + d = −8.

  4. Substitute d = −8 − a: ad = a(−8 − a) = −a2 − 8a = −(a2 + 8a + 16) + 16 = 16 − (a + 4)2.

  5. Since (a + 4)2 ≥ 0 for every real a, ad = 16 − (a + 4)2 ≤ 16, with equality exactly when a = −4 (which forces d = −4 too).

  6. So the maximum possible determinant is 16, attained at a = d = −4, b = 0.

Cross-check: Substituting a = d = −4, b = 0 gives A = [−4 0; 0 −4]; its trace is −4 + (−4) = −8 ✓ and its determinant is (−4)(−4) − 02 = 16 ✓. An independent check using eigenvalues: for a real symmetric matrix the eigenvalues λ1, λ2 are real, with λ1 + λ2 = trace = −8 and |A| = λ1λ2. Since the sum of the eigenvalues is fixed, their product is largest when λ1 = λ2 = −4, giving the same maximum product, 16.

So the maximum possible value of the determinant of the matrix is 16.

The nullity of a matrix is the difference between the number of columns and the rank.

Rank–Nullity Theorem (Linear Algebra)

For any matrix A of order m×n:

  • Nullity(A) = dimension of null space = number of free variables in Ax=0

  • n = number of columns in A

Total columns = pivot columns (rank) + free columns (nullity)

title: Ram Singh goes to Pushkar mela with Rs to buy
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: Ram Singh goes to the Pushkar mela with Rs 10,000, planning to spend the entire amount to buy exactly 100 animals. He finds that cows are sold at Rs 1,000 each, horses at Rs 300 each, and chickens at Rs 50 each. How many chickens should he buy?
solution:
Concept: This is a two-equation, three-unknown word problem restricted to non-negative integers (a linear Diophantine system) - one equation for the total number of animals, another for the total cost (the entire Rs 10,000 is spent). Combining the two by elimination reduces it to a single two-variable equation; since this is a multiple-choice question, the valid general solutions are then matched against the given options to pick the one that is actually offered.

  1. Let x = number of cows, y = number of horses, z = number of chickens.

  2. Total-animals equation: x + y + z = 100.

  3. Total-cost equation (the entire Rs 10,000 is spent): 1000x + 300y + 50z = 10000, which simplifies (dividing by 50) to 20x + 6y + z = 200.

  4. Subtracting the total-animals equation from the simplified cost equation eliminates z: (20x + 6y + z) - (x + y + z) = 200 - 100, giving 19x + 5y = 100.

  5. Since 5y is always a multiple of 5, 19x must also leave a remainder of 0 when divided by 5, so x must be a multiple of 5; and since 19x <= 100, the only possible values are x = 0 and x = 5.

  6. x = 0 gives y = 20 and z = 80; x = 5 gives 19(5) + 5y = 100, so y = 1 and z = 94.

  7. Among the given options (100, 90, 98, 94), only z = 94 is a valid solution to the system, so 94 is the answer.

Cross-check: 1000(5) + 300(1) + 50(94) = 5000 + 300 + 4700 = 10000, matching the full amount spent, and 5 + 1 + 94 = 100, matching the total count.

optionFeedback.html: Buying all 100 chickens costs 100 x 50 = Rs 5,000, leaving Rs 5,000 of the Rs 10,000 unspent - the entire amount is not spent, so this count does not meet the target.

With 90 chickens, the remaining 10 animals (cows and horses) would need to account for exactly Rs 5,500 at Rs 1,000 and Rs 300 each - no whole-number split of 10 animals between the two rates reaches that amount, so this count fails the cost constraint.

With 98 chickens, the remaining 2 animals (cows and horses) would need to account for exactly Rs 5,100 at Rs 1,000 and Rs 300 each - no whole-number split of 2 animals between the two rates reaches that amount, so this count fails the cost constraint.

With 94 chickens, the remaining 6 animals must account for exactly Rs 5,300 - the only whole-number split is 5 cows and 1 horse (5 x 1000 + 1 x 300 = 5300), which together with 94 chickens satisfies both the count and the full-spend constraints.

title: If are eigenvalues of matrix then the trace of is:

text: If λ1,λ2,λ3,...,λn are eigenvalues of a matrix A, then the trace of A is:
solution:
For any n×n matrix A, the trace tr(A) is defined as the sum of A's diagonal entries. A fundamental theorem of linear algebra states that tr(A) equals the sum of the eigenvalues of A, counted with algebraic multiplicity — because the trace is invariant under similarity transformations, and every square matrix (over the complex numbers) is similar to an upper-triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are exactly its eigenvalues.

Applying this to A with eigenvalues λ1,λ2,λ3,...,λn, the trace of A is λ1+λ2+λ3+...+λn.

As an independent check, expanding the characteristic polynomial det(λI − A) shows the coefficient of the (n−1)-degree term is −(λ1+λ2+...+λn), which equals −tr(A) — confirming the same identity.

text: What are the eigenvalues of the matrix given below:
solution:
Answer: The eigenvalues are 0, −2, −6.

  1. Form the matrix A − λI: A − λI = [[−λ, 2, 0], [0, −λ, 2], [0, −6, −8 − λ]].

  2. Compute the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI). Expand along the first column to get

    −λ · det([[−λ, 2], [−6, −8 − λ]]).

  3. Evaluate the 2×2 determinant: (−λ)(−8 − λ) − (2)(−6) = λ(8 + λ) + 12 = λ^2 + 8λ + 12.

  4. So the characteristic polynomial is −λ(λ^2 + 8λ + 12) = −λ(λ + 2)(λ + 6).

  5. Set this equal to zero and solve: λ = 0, λ = −2, λ = −6.

Therefore the eigenvalues are 0, −2, and −6.

Correct. Solve det(A − λI) = 0: A − λI = [[−λ, 2, 0],[0, −λ, 2],[0, −6, −8 − λ]]. Expanding gives −λ(λ^2 + 8λ + 12) = −λ(λ + 2)(λ + 6), so λ = 0, −2, −6.

title: Let be matrix: Then the sum of all elements of
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text:
Let M be a matrix:

Then the sum of all elements of M18 is ________.
solution:
Key idea: the given matrix M has the block form [[I, I], [0, I]], where I is the 3x3 identity matrix.

  • For any matrix N, the k-th power of the block matrix [I N; 0 I] is [I kN; 0 I].

  • Proof (by induction):

    Base case: k = 1 is trivial.

    Inductive step: assume (I N; 0 I)^k = (I kN; 0 I). Multiplying by (I N; 0 I) gives (I kN; 0 I)(I N; 0 I) = (I (kN+N); 0 I) = (I (k+1)N; 0 I).

Apply this with N = I to get M^18 = [[I, 18I], [0, I]].

Now compute the sum of all entries of M^18 by adding the sums of the four blocks:

  • Top-left block I (3x3 identity): sum = 3.

  • Top-right block 18I: sum = 18 × 3 = 54.

  • Bottom-left block 0: sum = 0.

  • Bottom-right block I: sum = 3.

Total sum = 3 + 54 + 0 + 3 = 60.

text:
Which among the following is not an eigenvector of the following matrix?

Note: Consider the options are in transposed order
solution:
Matrix: [-2 -4 2; -2 1 2; 4 2 5]

Key result: The characteristic polynomial factors give eigenvalues 3, -5, and 6. Verify each candidate vector by computing A·v and checking whether the result is a scalar multiple of v.

  • For [1, 6, 16]^T: A·[1,6,16]^T = [6, 36, 96]^T = 6·[1,6,16]^T, so this is an eigenvector (eigenvalue 6).

  • For [2, -1, 1]^T: A·[2,-1,1]^T = [2, -3, 11]^T, which is not a scalar multiple of [2, -1, 1]^T; therefore it is not an eigenvector. (The eigenvector corresponding to eigenvalue -5 is a multiple of [-2, -1, 1]^T.)

  • For [2, -3, -1]^T: A·[2,-3,-1]^T = [6, -9, -3]^T = 3·[2, -3, -1]^T, so this is an eigenvector (eigenvalue 3).

  • For [2, 6, -1]^T: A·[2,6,-1]^T = [-30, 0, 15]^T, which is not a scalar multiple of [2, 6, -1]^T; therefore it is not an eigenvector.

Conclusion: The vectors [2, -1, 1]^T and [2, 6, -1]^T are not eigenvectors of the given matrix. The vectors [1, 6, 16]^T and [2, -3, -1]^T are eigenvectors with eigenvalues 6 and 3 respectively.

Note on the original solution: The provided solution incorrectly identified [2, -1, 1]^T as an eigenvector. The corrected calculations above show it is not.

Multiply the matrix by [2, -1, 1]^T: A·[2,-1,1]^T = [2, -3, 11]^T, which is not a scalar multiple of [2, -1, 1]^T. Therefore [2, -1, 1]^T is not an eigenvector. (For reference, the eigenvector for eigenvalue -5 is a scalar multiple of [-2, -1, 1]^T, not [2, -1, 1]^T.)
Multiply the matrix by [2, -3, -1]^T: A·[2,-3,-1]^T = [6, -9, -3]^T = 3·[2, -3, -1]^T. Thus [2, -3, -1]^T is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3.
Multiply the matrix by [2, 6, -1]^T: A·[2,6,-1]^T = [-30, 0, 15]^T, which is not a scalar multiple of [2, 6, -1]^T. Therefore [2, 6, -1]^T is not an eigenvector.

title: Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that square matrix satisfies its own characteristic
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text:
Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that a square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. Consider a matrix:

The relation satisfied by the matrix A is ________.
solution:
Step 1: Compute the characteristic polynomial. Determinant |A - λI| = |3-λ 1; -2 -λ| = (3-λ)(-λ) - (1)(-2) = -3λ + λ^2 + 2 = λ^2 - 3λ + 2.

Step 2: Apply the Cayley–Hamilton theorem. Replacing λ by A gives A^2 - 3A + 2I = 0.

Step 3: Obtain the presented relation using invertibility. det(A) = 3·0 - 1·(-2) = 2 ≠ 0, so A is invertible. Multiply A^2 - 3A + 2I = 0 on the left by A^{-1} to get A - 3I + 2A^{-1} = 0.

Therefore the correct relation satisfied by A is A - 3I + 2A^{-1} = 0.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The characteristic polynomial gives A^2 - 3A + 2I = 0. If you multiply that by A^{-1} (allowed because A is invertible), you get A - 3I + 2A^{-1} = 0, not A + 3I + 2A^{-1} = 0. The signs on the A and I terms are wrong here.
Incorrect. Expanding (A - I)(A + 2I) gives A^2 + A - 2I, which does not match the characteristic polynomial replacement A^2 - 3A + 2I = 0. The coefficient of A is incorrect.

Incorrect. This has the wrong sign on the A^{-1} term. From the characteristic polynomial you get A^2 - 3A + 2I = 0, and after multiplying by A^{-1} the correct inverse-term sign is +2A^{-1}, giving A - 3I + 2A^{-1} = 0, not A - 3I - 2A^{-1} = 0.

Correct. The characteristic polynomial is λ^2 - 3λ + 2 = 0, so Cayley–Hamilton gives A^2 - 3A + 2I = 0. Since det(A) = 2 ≠ 0, A is invertible; multiplying that matrix equation on the left by A^{-1} yields A - 3I + 2A^{-1} = 0, which matches this relation.

title: Question 17806
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
solution:
Key idea: use eigenvectors of A to build eigenvectors of the block matrix.

Let A be 4×4 and let x be an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ (so Ax = λx). Consider the 8×8 block matrix P = [ A I ; I A ].

  • Take the vector [x; x]. Then

    P [x; x] = [A x + I x; I x + A x] = [(λ+1) x; (λ+1) x] = (λ+1) [x; x].

  • Take the vector [x; -x]. Then

    P [x; -x] = [A x - I x; I x - A x] = [(λ-1) x; -(λ-1) x] = (λ-1) [x; -x].

Thus for each eigenvalue λ of A the block matrix P has eigenvalues λ+1 and λ−1.

Apply this to the given eigenvalues of A: −5, −2, 1, 4.

  • For λ = −5: λ−1 = −6, λ+1 = −4.

  • For λ = −2: λ−1 = −3, λ+1 = −1.

  • For λ = 1: λ−1 = 0, λ+1 = 2.

  • For λ = 4: λ−1 = 3, λ+1 = 5.

So the eigenvalues of the block matrix are:

−6, −4, −3, −1, 0, 2, 3, 5

Conclusion: 2 is one of the eigenvalues (it equals 1+1).

optionFeedback.html: −5 is an eigenvalue of A, but the 8×8 block matrix has eigenvalues of the form λ+1 and λ−1 for each eigenvalue λ of A. For λ = −5 those are −4 and −6, so −5 is not an eigenvalue of the block matrix.
2 is an eigenvalue of the block matrix: take λ = 1 (an eigenvalue of A). Then λ+1 = 1+1 = 2, so the block matrix has 2 as an eigenvalue.
-7 is not an eigenvalue. For each eigenvalue λ of A we get λ+1 and λ−1; plugging λ ∈ {−5, −2, 1, 4} produces {−6, −4, −3, −1, 0, 2, 3, 5}. −7 does not appear.
1 is an eigenvalue of A but not of the block matrix. From λ = 1 we get λ+1 = 2 and λ−1 = 0; 1 itself does not occur among the values λ±1 for the given eigenvalues of A.

title: If the characteristic roots of are and the characteristic roots
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If the characteristic roots of A = [[3, 7], [2, 5]] are λ₁ and λ₂, what are the characteristic roots of A⁻¹ = [[5, −7], [−2, 3]]?
solution:
Concept

For an invertible matrix A, an eigenpair Av = λv with λ ≠ 0 becomes an eigenpair of A⁻¹ after applying the inverse: A⁻¹v = (1/λ)v.

Equivalently, inversion maps every eigenvalue λ to its reciprocal 1/λ while preserving the associated eigenvector.

Application — ordered working

  1. For A = [[3, 7], [2, 5]], det(A) = 3·5 − 7·2 = 1, so A is invertible.

  2. Using the 2 × 2 inverse formula, A⁻¹ = (1/det(A))[[5, −7], [−2, 3]] = [[5, −7], [−2, 3]], which is the second matrix in the stem.

  3. If Av = λ₁v for an eigenvector v, multiply by A⁻¹ to obtain v = λ₁A⁻¹v, hence A⁻¹v = (1/λ₁)v. The same argument maps λ₂ to 1/λ₂.

Cross-check

The determinant equals the product of the eigenvalues. Here det(A) = det(A⁻¹) = 1, and (1/λ₁)(1/λ₂) = 1/(λ₁λ₂) = 1, so the reciprocal pair has the required product.

Result

The characteristic roots of A⁻¹ are 1/λ₁ and 1/λ₂.

optionFeedback.html: For the pair (1/λ₁, 1/λ₂), the sum is (λ₁ + λ₂)/(λ₁λ₂) and the product is 1/(λ₁λ₂).
For the pair (λ₁ + λ₂, λ₁ − λ₂), the sum is 2λ₁ and the product is (λ₁ + λ₂)(λ₁ − λ₂).
For the pair (λ₁ + λ₂, |λ₁ − λ₂|), the sum is λ₁ + λ₂ + |λ₁ − λ₂| and the product is (λ₁ + λ₂)|λ₁ − λ₂|.
For the pair (2λ₁, 2λ₂), the sum is 2(λ₁ + λ₂) and the product is 4λ₁λ₂.

solution:
Solution: compute the LU factors and find u22.

  1. Assume L = [[1, 0], [l21, 1]] and U = [[u11, u12], [0, u22]].

  2. Multiply L and U to match the original matrix: LU = [[u11, u12], [l21*u11, l21*u12 + u22]] which must equal [[3, 2], [-4, 6]].

  3. Equate corresponding entries:

    • From (1,1): u11 = 3.

    • From (1,2): u12 = 2.

    • From (2,1): l21 * u11 = -4, so l21 = -4 / 3 = -4/3.

    • From (2,2): l21*u12 + u22 = 6, so u22 = 6 - l21*u12.

  4. Compute u22: u22 = 6 - (-4/3)*2 = 6 + 8/3 = (18 + 8)/3 = 26/3.

Final answer: u22 = 26/3

title: Question 802
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
solution:
Given the function f(x) = (4 - x^2) / (4x - x^3).

  • Factorize numerator and denominator:

    • Numerator: 4 - x^2 = (2 - x)(2 + x).

    • Denominator: 4x - x^3 = x(4 - x^2) = x(2 - x)(2 + x).

  • Simplify:

    Cancel the common factor (4 - x^2) = (2 - x)(2 + x). For x ≠ ±2 the function simplifies to f(x) = 1/x.

Discontinuities of the original function:

  • Find where the original denominator is zero: solve x(4 - x^2) = 0 → x = 0, x = 2, x = -2. These are points where the original expression is undefined.

  • Classify each discontinuity:

    • x = 0: numerator = 4 ≠ 0 while denominator = 0 → nonremovable (vertical) discontinuity.

    • x = 2 and x = -2: numerator and denominator both zero → removable discontinuities (holes). The simplified form 1/x gives limits 1/2 and -1/2 at these points respectively, but the original function is undefined there.

Conclusion:

  • The original function is discontinuous at three points: x = -2, x = 0, and x = 2.

  • Therefore the correct description is "Discontinuous at only three points."

  • The simplified form f(x) = 1/x (valid for x ≠ ±2) hides the removable holes at x = ±2 but does not change the fact that the original function is undefined there.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Check where the original denominator is zero: solve 4x - x^3 = 0 which gives x = 0 and x = ±2. All three points make the original expression undefined. Cancelling common factors can hide removable discontinuities at x = ±2, but the function is still undefined there in the original form, so there are three discontinuities, not two.

Incorrect. The denominator 4x - x^3 factors as x(4 - x^2) so it is zero at x = 0 and x = ±2. That gives three points where the original function is undefined, so it cannot be discontinuous at only one point.

Incorrect. The function is not continuous everywhere because the denominator equals zero for x = 0 and x = ±2, making the original expression undefined at those points. Two of these are removable (holes) and one is a nonremovable (vertical) discontinuity.

Correct. The denominator 4x - x^3 = x(4 - x^2) is zero at x = 0 and x = ±2, so the original function is undefined at three points. After cancelling the common factor you get 1/x for x ≠ ±2, which shows removable discontinuities (holes) at x = ±2 and a nonremovable discontinuity at x = 0.

title: Which one of the following functions is strictly bounded?
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: Which one of the following functions is strictly bounded?
solution:
Answer: 2 e^{-x^2} is the only bounded function.

Explanation:

  • For (3/2) x^2: As x → ±∞, (3/2) x^2 → ∞, so the function is not bounded above.

  • For 2 e^{-x^2}: The maximum occurs at x = 0 giving value 2, and as |x| → ∞ the value tends to 0 (but stays positive). Hence 0 < 2 e^{-x^2} ≤ 2, so it is bounded.

  • For e^{3x}: As x → ∞, e^{3x} → ∞, so the function is not bounded above (unbounded).

  • For x^3: As x → ∞ and x → −∞ the function tends to ∞ and −∞ respectively, so it is not bounded above or below.

optionFeedback.html: The function (3/2) x^2 grows without bound as |x| increases. As x → ±∞, (3/2) x^2 → ∞, so it is not bounded above and therefore not a bounded function.
The function 2 e^{-x^2} attains its maximum value 2 at x = 0 and tends to 0 as |x| → ∞ (never becoming negative). Thus 0 < 2 e^{-x^2} ≤ 2, so the function is bounded.
The function e^{3x} increases without bound as x → ∞ (e^{3x} → ∞), so it is not bounded above. Although it tends to 0 as x → −∞, that does not make it bounded overall.
The function x^3 tends to −∞ as x → −∞ and to ∞ as x → ∞, so it is unbounded both above and below and therefore not a bounded function.

title: Question 17796
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
solution:
Key idea: factor out the common denominator and use the formula for the sum of squares.

Combine the terms:

The expression equals (1^2+2^2+...+n^2)/(1 - n^3).

Use the sum formula:

  • 1^2+2^2+...+n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6.

So the expression becomes n(n+1)(2n+1) / (6(1 - n^3)).

Divide numerator and denominator by n^3 to evaluate the limit:

  • n(n+1)(2n+1) / (6(1 - n^3)) = (1+1/n)(2+1/n) / (6(1/n^3 - 1)).

Take the limit as n → ∞:

  1. Numerator (1+1/n)(2+1/n) → 1·2 = 2.

  2. Denominator 6(1/n^3 - 1) → 6(0 - 1) = -6.

title: Question 17829
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
solution:
Concept:

For a ratio f(x)/g(x) as x tends to infinity: if the numerator f(x) stays bounded between two fixed numbers for every x, while the denominator g(x) grows without bound, then the ratio is squeezed between two bounds that both tend to 0. This is the Squeeze (Sandwich) Theorem: if g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a point and both g(x) and h(x) tend to the same limit L, then f(x) also tends to L.

Applying it here:

  1. For every real x, sin x is bounded: -1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1.

  2. Dividing throughout by x (positive as x tends to infinity, so the inequality direction is preserved): -1/x ≤ sin x / x ≤ 1/x.

  3. As x tends to infinity, both bounds -1/x and 1/x tend to 0.

  4. By the squeeze theorem, the sandwiched expression sin x / x must also tend to 0.

Cross-check:

Independently: sin x / x is the product of a bounded oscillating factor (sin x, always within [-1, 1]) and a factor 1/x that itself tends to 0. A bounded quantity multiplied by a quantity tending to 0 also tends to 0 — the same conclusion as the squeeze-theorem derivation above, confirming the result.

Therefore, the limit equals 0.

optionFeedback.html: Since sin x always stays bounded between -1 and 1 for every real x, while the denominator x grows without bound as x tends to infinity, the ratio sin x / x is squeezed between -1/x and 1/x, both of which tend to 0. By the squeeze theorem, the ratio tends to 0.

This assumes sin x settles near a fixed value close to 1 as x grows large, but sin x never settles — it keeps oscillating between -1 and 1 forever. A numerator that stays bounded while being divided by an ever-growing denominator cannot produce a ratio tending to 1.

This assumes the oscillation of sin x prevents any limit from existing, but that is not the case here: dividing an always-bounded numerator by a denominator that grows without bound squeezes the ratio down to one definite limiting value, so the limit does exist.

This assumes the true limiting value is not among the given choices, but applying the squeeze theorem to this ratio shows it settles to one specific finite value that is indeed one of the given choices.

title: Find the sum of all the terms in the series
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: Find the sum of all the terms in the series 1, 1/2, 1/4, ...... (an infinite geometric series).
solution:
Concept: An infinite geometric series with first term a and common ratio r, where |r| < 1, converges to a finite sum given by S = a / (1 - r). This follows from the partial-sum formula Sn = a(1 - rn) / (1 - r): as n grows without bound and |r| < 1, rn approaches 0, so the partial sums approach a / (1 - r).

  1. Identify the first term and common ratio from the given series 1, 1/2, 1/4, ......: a = 1, and r = 1/2 (each term is half the one before it).

  2. Confirm convergence: since |r| = 1/2 < 1, the series has a finite sum, so the formula S = a / (1 - r) applies.

  3. Substitute the values into the formula: S = 1 / (1 - 1/2) = 1 / (1/2) = 2.

Cross-check: the running partial sums — 1, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875, 1.9375, ...... — steadily approach 2 without ever reaching or exceeding it, confirming the formula's result.

optionFeedback.html: This is the exact sum of the infinite geometric series, obtained from the standard formula S = a / (1 - r) with first term a = 1 and common ratio r = 1/2: S = 1 / (1 - 1/2) = 1 / (1/2) = 2.

This value overshoots the true convergent sum. It would arise from misapplying the infinite-series formula, for example by treating the common ratio in a way that inflates the denominator's contribution instead of correctly using 1/2, which pushes the computed total above the actual limit.

This value is too large for the actual limit of the series. It could result from mistaking the sum of the infinite series for some other quantity related to the terms (such as a scaled first term) rather than carrying out the convergence formula correctly.

The sum can, in fact, be determined. Each term here is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a constant ratio whose absolute value is less than 1 (here, 1/2), and any such series is guaranteed to converge to a single finite value — so 'cannot be determined' does not apply.

solution:
Key idea: a rational function can only be discontinuous where its denominator is zero, unless the numerator has the same factor that cancels the denominator zero.

Conclusion: The function is not continuous at x = -2/3 and x = 1.

solution:
Concept

A function f is continuous at a point x = a only when all three of these exist and are equal: the value f(a), the left-hand limit (LHL) as x → a⁻, and the right-hand limit (RHL) as x → a⁺. If even one is missing or unequal, f is discontinuous there.

Evaluate the three quantities for the piecewise rule that uses (x + 3)/3 below 3, x − 1 above 3, and the value 2 at the point itself:

  1. LHL: as x → 3⁻ use (x + 3)/3, giving (3 + 3)/3 = 2.

  2. RHL: as x → 3⁺ use x − 1, giving 3 − 1 = 2.

  3. Point value: f(3) = 2 is defined directly.

Cross-check

All three agree: LHL = RHL = f(3) = 2, so the three-part test is satisfied and this rule is continuous at x = 3. The others fail it — a fixed point value that disagrees with the common limit, a rule that never assigns a value at x = 3, and a rule whose denominator collapses to 0 at x = 3.

Result: the continuous function is the one defined by (x + 3)/3 for x < 3, x − 1 for x > 3, and 2 at x = 3.

title: If the radius of the circle changes at the rate
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If the radius of a circle changes at the rate of −2/π m/sec, at what rate does the circle's area change when the radius is 10 m?
solution:
Concept: When two quantities are tied together by an equation, differentiating that equation with respect to time ties their rates together as well. A circle’s area and radius satisfy A = πr2, so by the chain rule dA/dt = (dA/dr)·(dr/dt) = 2πr·(dr/dt). The factor 2πr is the circumference at that instant, and dA/dt inherits the sign of dr/dt — a radius that is shrinking forces a shrinking area.

Application: here the radial rate is dr/dt = −2/π m/sec and the instant of interest is r = 10 m.

  1. Write the relation between the quantities: A = πr2.

  2. Differentiate both sides with respect to time t using the chain rule: dA/dt = 2πr·(dr/dt).

  3. Substitute the radius at the required instant, r = 10 m: dA/dt = 2π(10)·(dr/dt) = 20π·(dr/dt).

  4. Substitute the given radial rate, dr/dt = −2/π m/sec: dA/dt = 20π × (−2/π).

  5. Cancel π: dA/dt = 20 × (−2) = −40.

  6. Attach the units, (m) × (m/sec) = m2/sec: dA/dt = −40 m2/sec.

Cross-check: both the dimension and the size agree. The factor 2πr at r = 10 m is the circumference 20π m, and a length in metres multiplied by a radial speed in m/sec gives m2/sec, which is exactly the dimension of an area rate. For the size, 20π ≈ 62·8 and the radial speed has magnitude 2/π ≈ 0·64, whose product is about 40; the radius is decreasing, so the area rate carries a minus sign.

Hence the area of the circle is changing at −40 m2/sec — that is, shrinking by 40 m2 every second.

title: Find the minimum value of the given function f(x,y)=x3+y3-3xy+81, over
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: Find the minimum value of the given function f(x,y)=x3+y3-3xy+81, over the positive real domain is
solution:
Step 1: rewrite the function.

f(x,y) = x^3 + y^3 - 3xy + 81 = 80 + (x^3 + y^3 + 1 - 3xy).

Step 2: apply the three-variable identity (Schur-type factorization).

For the numbers x, y, 1 we have

x^3 + y^3 + 1 - 3xy = 1/2 (x + y + 1) [ (x - y)^2 + (y - 1)^2 + (1 - x)^2 ].

Each squared term is nonnegative, and for positive x and y the factor (x + y + 1) is positive, so the entire product is ≥ 0.

Conclusion: therefore f(x,y) ≥ 80 for all positive x,y, with equality exactly when (x - y) = 0, (y - 1) = 0 and (1 - x) = 0, i.e. at x = y = 1.

Thus the minimum value of f over the positive real domain is 80, attained at (1,1).

title: Point on curve is said to be an extremum if
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: A point on a curve is said to be an extremum if it is a local minimum or a local maximum. The number of distinct extrema for the curve 3x4 − 8x3 + 6x2 + 7 is
solution:
A critical point is where the first derivative vanishes, but it is a genuine local extremum only if the derivative's sign actually flips across that point (the first-derivative test). If a root of the derivative has even multiplicity, the sign does not change there, and that point is a stationary/inflection point, not an extremum.

  1. Differentiate y = 3x4 - 8x3 + 6x2 + 7 to get y' = 12x3 - 24x2 + 12x.

  2. Factorise: y' = 12x(x2 - 2x + 1) = 12x(x-1)2.

  3. Solve y' = 0, which gives x = 0 (a simple root) and x = 1 (a double root).

  4. Sign-test around x = 0: at x = -0.1, y' < 0; at x = 0.1, y' > 0. The sign flips from negative to positive, so x = 0 is a local minimum.

  5. Sign-test around x = 1: at x = 0.9, y' > 0; at x = 1.1, y' > 0. The sign stays positive on both sides, so there is no flip, and x = 1 is not an extremum — it is a stationary inflection point caused by the squared factor.

  6. Conclusion: only one root produces a genuine sign change, so the curve has exactly 1 distinct extremum.

Cross-check (second-derivative test): y'' = 36x2 - 48x + 12. At x = 0, y'' = 12 > 0, independently confirming the local minimum. At x = 1, y'' = 0 (inconclusive by itself), which is consistent with x = 1 not being a genuine extremum — corroborating the first-derivative-test conclusion via an independent route.

optionFeedback.html: Among the two critical points of this quartic, only x = 0 produces a genuine sign change in the derivative — the other, x = 1, is a repeated root where the derivative's sign does not flip. Since exactly one critical point qualifies as an extremum under the sign-change test, the curve has exactly 1 distinct extremum.

This assumes that every point where the derivative vanishes is automatically an extremum. That assumption is not reliable — a critical point only qualifies as a genuine local minimum or maximum if the derivative's sign actually flips across it (the first-derivative test); a critical point that fails this test does not count as an extremum, no matter how many roots the derivative appears to have.

This assumes a degree-3 derivative automatically produces three separate extrema. But a cubic derivative sets only an upper bound on the number of critical points, and it can carry a repeated root — even where a root is genuinely distinct, it must still pass the sign-change test before it can be counted as an extremum; the raw degree of the derivative does not by itself fix how many extrema the curve has.

A quartic's derivative is a cubic, and a cubic polynomial can have at most 3 real roots — never 4. So 4 distinct critical points, let alone 4 extrema, is algebraically impossible for this curve regardless of how the sign analysis turns out.

solution:
Concept

To integrate a polynomial times sin x or cos x, use integration by parts (∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du), lowering the polynomial's degree by one each pass: ∫ xn sin x dx and ∫ xn cos x dx feed into each other, so apply parts repeatedly until the polynomial vanishes.

Application

Find the antiderivative of x3 sin x by parts, reducing the power of x at each step:

  1. ∫ x3 sin x dx: take u = x3, dv = sin x dx, so it equals −x3 cos x + 3 ∫ x2 cos x dx.

  2. ∫ x2 cos x dx = x2 sin x − 2 ∫ x sin x dx.

  3. ∫ x sin x dx = −x cos x + ∫ cos x dx = −x cos x + sin x.

  4. Back-substitute: ∫ x2 cos x dx = x2 sin x + 2x cos x − 2 sin x.

  5. Hence ∫ x3 sin x dx = −x3 cos x + 3x2 sin x + 6x cos x − 6 sin x + C.

  6. Evaluate from 0 to π. At x = π: sin π = 0 and cos π = −1, leaving −π3(−1) + 6π(−1) = π3 − 6π. At x = 0 every term has a factor of x or sin x, so it is 0.

Therefore ∫₀^π x3 sin x dx = π3 − 6π.

solution:
Concept

The composite trapezoidal rule approximates a definite integral by joining consecutive data points with straight chords, so each strip becomes a trapezium. For n equal sub-intervals of width h, the estimate is

∫ f dx ≈ h × [ (ffirst + flast) / 2 + (sum of all interior f-values) ]

Equivalently, the two end ordinates get weight 1 and every interior ordinate gets weight 2, all multiplied by h/2.

The eleven tabulated abscissae are equally spaced, so the step size is fixed:

  1. Step size: h = (3.0 − 0) / 10 = 0.3, giving 10 strips across the eleven points.

  3. Interior ordinates (the nine middle values): 0.09 + 0.36 + 0.81 + 1.44 + 2.25 + 3.24 + 4.41 + 5.76 + 7.29 = 25.65.

  4. Combine: integral ≈ h × (4.5 + 25.65) = 0.3 × 30.15 = 9.045.

Because x2 is convex, the chords lie above the curve, so the trapezoidal estimate must be slightly larger than 9.000 — and 9.045 is indeed just above it, confirming the arithmetic. solution:
When two events A and B are independent, the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability of the other occurring.
By definition in probability theory, the joint probability P(A ∩ B), which represents the likelihood that both events occur simultaneously, is calculated by multiplying their individual probabilities.
Therefore, for independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
This multiplicative rule distinguishes independent events from mutually exclusive events, where the intersection probability is zero. Option A (P(A) + P(B)) applies to mutually exclusive events for their union, not intersection.
Option C (P(A) − P(B)) and Option D (P(A) / P(B)) do not represent standard probability rules for intersections.

title: The probability of solving question by Jindal is while that
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: The probability of solving a question by Jindal is 3/5 while that of not solving it by Avi is 1/4. What is the probability that the problem be solved?
solution:
To find the probability that the problem is solved, it is often easiest to calculate the probability that the problem is not solved by either person and subtract that from 1.

Step-by-Step Calculation
Determine individual probabilities:

Probability Jindal solves the problem: P(Jindal) = 3/5

Probability Jindal fails: P(Jindal fails) = 1 - 3/5 = 2/5

Probability Avi does not solve the problem: P(Avi fails) = 1/4

Probability Avi solves the problem: P(Avi) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4

Calculate the probability that neither solves the problem:
Since the two events are independent, the probability that both fail is the product of their individual failure probabilities:

P(Neither solves) = P(Jindal fails) × P(Avi fails)

P(Neither solves) = (2/5) × (1/4) = 2/20 = 1/10

Calculate the probability that the problem is solved:
The problem is solved if at least one of them succeeds, which is the complement of neither solving it:

P(Problem solved) = 1 - P(Neither solves)

P(Problem solved) = 1 - 1/10 = 9/10

Correct Option
Option B: 9/10

title: Question in mathematics is given to three students and whose
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: A question in mathematics is given to three students P, Q and R whose chances of solving are 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 respectively. What is the probability that the problem will be solved?
solution:
Step-by-Step Solution

Given:

Probability that P solves the problem = 1/3
Probability that Q solves the problem = 1/4
Probability that R solves the problem = 1/5

We need to find the probability that the problem is solved, i.e., at least one student solves it.

Step 1: Find the probability that each student fails
P fails = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3
Q fails = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4
R fails = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5
Step 2: Find the probability that none of them solves the problem

Assuming their attempts are independent,

Probability (none solve)
= (2/3) × (3/4) × (4/5)

= 2/5

= 0.4

Step 3: Find the probability that at least one solves the problem

Probability (at least one solves)

= 1 − Probability (none solve)

= 1 − 2/5

= 3/5

= 0.6

Final Answer: 0.6

0.4 is the probability that none of the students solves the problem.

The question asks for the probability that the problem will be solved, which means at least one student must solve it.

Common Mistake:
Stopping after calculating the probability of failure of all three students and forgetting to take the complement.

Why it is correct:

First calculate the probability that all three students fail:

(2/3) × (3/4) × (4/5) = 2/5 = 0.4

Then use the complement rule:

Probability (at least one solves)

= 1 − 0.4

= 0.6

This correctly gives the probability that the problem is solved by at least one student.

Why it is incorrect:

This value does not result from the correct probability calculation.

A common error is adding probabilities directly:

1/3 + 1/4 + 1/5 = 47/60 ≈ 0.783

which is close to 0.8.

However, direct addition is not valid because the events overlap. More than one student can solve the problem simultaneously, causing double-counting.

Key Concept:
For independent events, use the complement method rather than simply adding the probabilities.

Why it is incorrect:

0.7 is not obtained from the correct complement calculation.

The correct approach is:

Probability (none solve) = 0.4

Probability (at least one solves) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6

Therefore, 0.7 overestimates the required probability.

Key Concept:

text: Consider Vamshi decides to toss a fair coin repeatedly until he gets a tail. He makes at most 4 tosses. The value of variance (T) is ____ (where T denotes the number of tosses).
solution:
Key idea: find the probability distribution of T (number of tosses) accounting for the fact that he stops after at most 4 tosses.

  • P(T = 1) = probability of tail on 1st toss = 1/2.

  • P(T = 2) = head then tail = (1/2)*(1/2) = 1/4.

  • P(T = 3) = HH then tail = (1/2)^3 = 1/8.

  • P(T = 4) = (first tail on 4th) OR (no tail in first 4 tosses) = (1/2)^4 + (1/2)^4 = 2*(1/16) = 1/8.

  • E[T] = 1*(1/2) + 2*(1/4) + 3*(1/8) + 4*(1/8) = 1/2 + 1/2 + 3/8 + 4/8 = 15/8.

Compute E[T^2]:

Therefore the correct variance is 71/64 (approximately 1.1094).

text: The probability that a leap year selected at random will contain either 53 Sundays or 53 Mondays is
solution:
A leap year has 366 days = 52 complete weeks + 2 extra days. Those 2 extra days always fall as a consecutive pair, and every one of the 7 possible weekday pairs is equally likely. A given weekday gets a 53rd occurrence in that year exactly when it is one of the two extra days -- so for two such events, the chance of either happening is found with the inclusion-exclusion rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).

  2. 53 Sundays occur exactly when the pair includes Sunday: (Saturday, Sunday) and (Sunday, Monday) -- 2 of the 7 pairs, so P(53 Sundays) = 2/7.

  3. 53 Mondays occur exactly when the pair includes Monday: (Sunday, Monday) and (Monday, Tuesday) -- 2 of the 7 pairs, so P(53 Mondays) = 2/7.

  4. Sunday and Monday are adjacent days of the week, so exactly one pair -- (Sunday, Monday) -- contains both, giving the overlap P(53 Sundays and 53 Mondays) = 1/7.

  5. By inclusion-exclusion, P(53 Sundays or 53 Mondays) = 2/7 + 2/7 - 1/7 = 3/7.

Cross-check by counting directly: the pairs that give 53 Sundays or 53 Mondays are (Saturday, Sunday), (Sunday, Monday), and (Monday, Tuesday) -- 3 of the 7 pairs -- which confirms 3/7.

Answer: 3/7

When an event (here, a correct answer) can arise from two mutually exclusive causes, the probability that one particular cause produced it, given the event happened, equals that cause's contribution divided by the total probability of the event: P(cause | event) = P(cause)·P(event | cause) / P(event).

Setup

Let K = the student knows the answer and G = the student guesses. P(K) = 90% = 9/10, so P(G) = 1 − 9/10 = 1/10. A known answer is always correct: P(correct | K) = 1. A pure guess among four options with one correct: P(correct | G) = 1/4.

Working

  1. Total probability of a correct answer (law of total probability): P(correct) = P(K)·P(correct | K) + P(G)·P(correct | G).

  2. Substitute: P(correct) = (9/10)(1) + (1/10)(1/4) = 9/10 + 1/40 = 36/40 + 1/40 = 37/40.

  3. Apply Bayes for the guessing cause: P(G | correct) = [P(G)·P(correct | G)] / P(correct) = (1/40) / (37/40).

  4. Simplify: (1/40) / (37/40) = 1/37.

Cross-check

The complementary posterior is P(K | correct) = (9/10) / (37/40) = 36/37. Since 1/37 + 36/37 = 1, the two posteriors are consistent.

Result

Given a correct answer, the probability the student was guessing is 1/37.

To find that you must apply Bayes' theorem and not use P(correct) directly.

title: What is the probability of observing exactly successes in trials
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: What is the probability of observing exactly k successes in n trials in a binomial distribution with parameter p ?
solution:
Concept

The binomial distribution models the number of successes in n independent trials, each with a constant success probability p. The probability of observing exactly k successes equals the probability of one fixed ordering of k successes and (n − k) failures, multiplied by the number of distinct orderings in which those k successes can occur.

Application

  1. Probability of one fixed ordering: because trials are independent, one specific sequence with exactly k successes (each with probability p) and (n − k) failures (each with probability 1 − p) has probability pk(1 − p)n−k.

  2. Count the orderings: the k successes can occupy any k of the n trial positions, and the number of ways to choose those positions is the combination C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!).

  3. Combine: multiplying the probability of one ordering by the number of equally likely orderings gives the probability of exactly k successes: P(X = k) = C(n, k)·pk·(1 − p)n−k.

Cross-check

Setting n = 1 makes C(1, k) equal to 1 for k = 0 or k = 1, so the formula reduces to the plain single-trial probabilities (1 − p) and p — consistent with a binomial distribution being n repeated Bernoulli trials. Summing P(X = k) over k = 0 to n also reproduces the binomial expansion of (p + (1 − p))n = 1, confirming the probabilities across all k values add up correctly.

Why the other forms fall short

  • p(1 − p)k has no combination factor at all and does not even track the total number of trials n in its exponents.

  • pk(1 − p)n−k correctly captures one ordering but has no combination factor, so it never counts how many orderings of k successes among n trials exist.

  • nCk·pn(1 − p)k keeps a combination factor but the two exponents are interchanged, so they no longer track which count (successes or failures) belongs to which base.

Result: P(X = k) = C(n, k)·pk·(1 − p)n−k — the combination term multiplied by p raised to the successes count and (1 − p) raised to the failures count.

optionFeedback.html: This expression has no combination factor and its exponent structure does not scale with the total number of trials n — it only ever tracks a single power of p times (1 − p) raised to k, so it cannot represent the probability across n independent trials.

This expression represents the probability of one specific arrangement of k successes and (n − k) failures among n trials, but it does not account for the fact that those k successes can occur in more than one arrangement across the n trials — try counting how many different orders of successes and failures are possible for a small case such as n = 3, k = 2, and compare it to what this expression gives.

This expression retains the combination factor nCk needed to count arrangements, but its exponents on p and (1 − p) do not correctly correspond to the number of successes and the number of failures respectively — the mismatch shows up if you check this expression against a small case such as n = 2, k = 1.

This expression pairs the combination factor nCk with p raised to the successes count k and (1 − p) raised to the failures count (n − k), matching how the binomial probability mass function counts and weights every ordering of exactly k successes among n independent trials.

title: Bag contains gel pens, ink pens and sketch pens. If
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text:

A bag contains 2 gel pens, 4 ink pens and 6 sketch pens. If two pens were chosen at random what is the probability that one is an ink pen and one is a sketch pen?
solution:
Concept: When items are drawn from a bag without replacement, the probability of getting a specific mix across categories equals (the number of ways to choose the required items from each category) divided by (the number of ways to choose the same total count of items from the whole bag) — a single simultaneous draw uses combinations (nCr), not permutations, because order does not matter. When an event needs one item from EACH of two specified categories, the favourable count is the PRODUCT of the two individual category counts, not their sum.

Application:

  1. Total pens in the bag = 2 gel + 4 ink + 6 sketch = 12 pens.

  2. Total ways to choose any 2 pens out of 12, ignoring order: C(12,2) = (12 × 11) / (2 × 1) = 66.

  3. Favourable ways: 1 ink pen chosen from the 4 ink pens gives C(4,1) = 4 ways, and 1 sketch pen chosen from the 6 sketch pens gives C(6,1) = 6 ways; by the multiplication rule, favourable pairs = 4 × 6 = 24.

  4. Probability = favourable ÷ total = 24 / 66, which simplifies (divide numerator and denominator by 6) to 4/11.

Cross-check with sequential probability: P(ink first, then sketch) = (4/12) × (6/11) = 24/132, and P(sketch first, then ink) = (6/12) × (4/11) = 24/132. Since either order gives one ink pen and one sketch pen, add the two: 24/132 + 24/132 = 48/132 = 4/11 — the same result as the combinations method.

Answer: The probability that one pen is an ink pen and one is a sketch pen is 4/11.

Step-by-Step Solution
To find the expected value of a function of a random variable, E[g(X)], we use the integral of that function multiplied by the probability density function (PDF) of the random variable.

Identify the PDF: For a continuous uniform distribution on the interval [0, 1], the PDF f(x) is defined as:
f(x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and 0 otherwise.

Set up the integral: We want to find E[X³].
E[X³] = ∫₀¹ x³ * f(x) dx
E[X³] = ∫₀¹ x³ * 1 dx

Integrate:
Using the power rule for integration, ∫ xⁿ dx = x^(n+1) / (n+1):
E[X³] = [x⁴ / 4] evaluated from 0 to 1.

Evaluate:
E[X³] = (1⁴ / 4) - (0⁴ / 4)
E[X³] = (1 / 4) - 0 = 1 / 4

title: Find the variance in uniform distribution if is uniformly distributed
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Continuous Probability Distribution, Random Variables & Expected Value
text: Find the variance in uniform distribution if X is uniformly distributed over (5, 30) ?
solution:
Variance Formula Recap
For a continuous uniform distribution over the interval (a, b), the formula is:

Variance = ((b - a)²) / 12

Step-by-Step Calculation
Identify the parameters: Here, a = 5 and b = 30.

Calculate the range: b - a = 30 - 5 = 25.

Square the range: 25² = 625.

Divide by 12: 625 / 12 ≈ 52.083.

Why this is a Continuous Distribution
The distribution is continuous because the variable can take on any real number within the interval (5, 30). Because there are infinitely many values between 5 and 30, we use a Probability Density Function (PDF) to represent it, which is represented by a horizontal line over the interval on a graph.

Comparison with Discrete Uniform Distribution
If the question asked about a discrete uniform distribution (like selecting a random whole number from 5 to 30), the formula would change to:

Variance = ((n² - 1) / 12)

Where 'n' is the number of possible outcomes. In that scenario, the variance would be calculated very differently because you are dealing with distinct, countable points rather than a continuous range.

title: Compute the Median for the exponential distribution with parameter
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Continuous Probability Distribution, Random Variables & Expected Value
text: Compute the Median for the exponential distribution with parameter λ:
solution:
Step-by-Step Solution
To find the median (m) of a continuous probability distribution, we must find the value where the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) equals 0.5.

Identify the CDF: For an exponential distribution with parameter λ, the CDF is:
F(x) = 1 - e^(-λx)

Set the CDF to 0.5: To find the median (m), we solve:
1 - e^(-λm) = 0.5

Rearrange the equation:
e^(-λm) = 1 - 0.5
e^(-λm) = 0.5

Take the natural logarithm (log) of both sides:
-λm = log(0.5)

Simplify:
Since log(0.5) is the same as -log(2):
-λm = -log(2)
m = log(2) / λ

title: Which of the following statements can be inferred about the
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Continuous Probability Distribution, Random Variables & Expected Value
text: Which of the following statements can be inferred about the Mean, Median, and Mode of the normal distribution P(x) for a variable x ?
solution:
Step-by-Step Solution
To determine the relationship between the mean, median, and mode for a normal distribution, we look at the shape of the curve:

Symmetry: A normal distribution is perfectly symmetric about its center.

Mean (Average): Because the distribution is perfectly balanced, the arithmetic average (mean) is located exactly at the center of the distribution.

Median (Middle Value): Since the distribution is symmetric, exactly 50% of the data lies to the left of the center and 50% lies to the right, meaning the median also falls exactly at the center.

Mode (Most Frequent Value): The peak of the normal distribution curve represents the highest probability density, which is at the center. Thus, the mode also coincides with the center.

Because all three measures—the mean, the median, and the mode—are located at the same central point, they are equal: MEAN = MEDIAN = MODE.

text: If x and y are independent Gaussian random variables with mean 0 and the same variance, their joint probability density function is:
solution:
Concept

For independent continuous random variables, the joint probability density factorizes into the product of the marginal densities.

Thus, independence determines the factorization rule; the common mean and variance specify the marginals but do not alter that rule.

Application

Here x and y are explicitly independent, so substitute their marginal densities into the factorization identity: p(x,y) = p(x) p(y).

Contrast

  • p(x) + p(y) adds marginal densities; addition is not the independence factorization.

  • p(x+y) is a density evaluated at the sum and is not a joint density in the two variables.

  • p(x)p(y) + p(x) adds an extra marginal-density term to the product.

Cross-check

The product is normalized because integrating p(x)p(y) over both variables separates into two marginal integrals, each equal to 1. Therefore the joint density is p(x,y) = p(x)p(y).

title: There are cards in standard deck with four sets {Hearts,
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: There are 52 cards in a standard deck with four sets {Hearts, Spades, Club, Diamond}. How many cards should be selected from that deck to guarantee that at least three cards of the same set are taken_______________
solution:
Answer: 9 cards.

Reasoning (pigeonhole principle):

  • To avoid having three cards of the same suit, you can take at most 2 cards from each suit.

  • With 4 suits, that maximum is 2 × 4 = 8 cards without getting three of any suit.

  • Picking one more card (8 + 1 = 9) forces some suit to have at least three cards.

Therefore, you must select 9 cards to guarantee at least three cards from the same suit.

solution:
To determine the percentage of data lying within one standard deviation of the mean in a normal distribution, we refer to the Empirical Rule (also known as the 68-95-99.7 rule).

Analysis of the Empirical Rule
The Empirical Rule provides a standardized way to understand the spread of data in a normal distribution:

Within one standard deviation (±1σ): Approximately 68% of the data lies within one standard deviation from the mean.

Within two standard deviations (±2σ): Approximately 95% of the data lies within two standard deviations from the mean.

Within three standard deviations (±3σ): Approximately 99.7% of the data lies within three standard deviations from the mean.

To understand the characteristics of a binomial distribution, it helps to identify the specific criteria a process must meet to qualify as one.

Characteristics of a Binomial Distribution
A binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of trials. For a distribution to be binomial, it must satisfy these conditions:

Fixed Number of Trials: There is a predetermined number of trials (n).

Two Possible Outcomes: Each trial results in only two mutually exclusive outcomes, commonly referred to as "success" or "failure." * Independent Trials: The outcome of one trial does not affect the outcome of any other trial.

Constant Probability: The probability of success (p) remains constant for each trial.

text:
Set={1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4}

Evaluate the following expression for the above given set of numbers:

3(mean) + 2(mode) – 6(median).
solution:
For any data set: the mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values; the mode is the value that occurs with the greatest frequency; and the median is the middle value when the data is sorted in increasing order — for an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle values.

  1. Sort the set: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4 — it has 10 values, already arranged in increasing order.

  2. Mode: the value 4 occurs four times, more often than any other value in the set, so Mode = 4.

  3. Median: with 10 (even) values, the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values. Both the 5th and 6th values are 3, so Median = (3 + 3) / 2 = 3.

  4. Mean: the sum of all ten values is 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 30, and there are 10 values, so Mean = 30 / 10 = 3.

  5. Substitute into the expression: 3(mean) + 2(mode) – 6(median) = 3(3) + 2(4) – 6(3) = 9 + 8 – 18 = –1.

As an independent check, group the values by frequency: one 1, two 2s, three 3s, and four 4s, giving a sum of 1(1) + 2(2) + 3(3) + 4(4) = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30 — the same total used for the mean, confirming Mean = 3. Recomputing the expression term by term, 9 + 8 = 17, and 17 – 18 = –1, confirming the result.

So the expression evaluates to –1.

Recompute the median using the correct middle positions, then substitute all three measures into the expression again.

With the mode, median, and mean correctly identified as 4, 3, and 3 for this data set, substituting into 3(mean) + 2(mode) – 6(median) gives 3(3) + 2(4) – 6(3) = 9 + 8 – 18, which is the value shown here.

title: If mode of the following data is then the value

text: If mode of the following data is 6, then the value of k in the 3, 8, 6, 7, 1, 6, 10, 6, 7, 2k + 4, 9, 7, and 13 is:
solution:
Concept: The mode of a data set is the value that occurs with the highest frequency. If two or more values tie for the highest frequency, the data set has more than one mode (it is bimodal/multimodal) rather than a single, unique mode — so for a data set to have exactly one mode, that value must occur strictly more often than every other value.

Applying this to the given data:

  1. The data set is 3, 8, 6, 7, 1, 6, 10, 6, 7, 2k + 4, 9, 7, and 13, which contains twelve fixed numbers plus one variable term, 2k + 4.

  2. Counting the fixed values: 6 occurs 3 times, 7 occurs 3 times, and every other fixed value (3, 8, 1, 10, 9, 13) occurs only once.

  3. Since 6 and 7 are tied at 3 occurrences each before the variable term is counted, 6 can only become the unique mode if the variable term itself takes the value 6 (any other value either creates a new tie elsewhere or leaves 6 and 7 still tied at three).

  4. Set up the equation for the variable term: 2k + 4 = 6.

  5. Solve for k: 2k = 6 - 4 = 2, so k = 1.

Cross-check: Substituting k = 1 back into the data set gives 2(1) + 4 = 6, so the data becomes 3, 8, 6, 7, 1, 6, 10, 6, 7, 6, 9, 7, and 13 — 6 now occurs 4 times while 7 still occurs 3 times, and every other value occurs once. 6 is now strictly the most frequent value, confirming a unique mode of 6.

Therefore, k = 1.

Substituting k = 10 gives 2k + 4 = 24. This value of k does not make 6 the mode of the data set.
Substituting k = 1 gives 2k + 4 = 6. This value of k makes 6 the mode of the data set.
Substituting k = 50 gives 2k + 4 = 104. This value of k does not make 6 the mode of the data set.

title: Find the median of the following data.
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Mean, Median, and Mode for ungrouped data
text:
Find the median of the following data.
1/2, 4/5, 7/12, 4/3, 5/6, 6/7, 2/3
solution:
Concept

The median is the middle observation of a data set once the values are arranged in order of size. For n observations written in ascending order the median is the ((n + 1)/2)-th term when n is odd, and the average of the (n/2)-th and (n/2 + 1)-th terms when n is even. Because the median is defined by rank, sorting the data is the first and essential step; the order in which the values happen to be printed carries no information.

Application

  1. Count the observations. The list 1/2, 4/5, 7/12, 4/3, 5/6, 6/7, 2/3 contains n = 7 values, and 7 is odd, so the median is the (7 + 1)/2 = 4th term of the sorted list.

  2. Pick a common denominator so that the fractions can be compared exactly. The denominators are 2, 5, 12, 3, 6 and 7, and their LCM is 420, since 420 = 22 × 3 × 5 × 7.

  3. Rewrite each value over 420: 1/2 = 210/420, 4/5 = 336/420, 7/12 = 245/420, 4/3 = 560/420, 5/6 = 350/420, 6/7 = 360/420 and 2/3 = 280/420.

  4. With equal denominators, comparing the fractions is just comparing the numerators: 210 < 245 < 280 < 336 < 350 < 360 < 560, so the data in ascending order is 1/2, 7/12, 2/3, 4/5, 5/6, 6/7, 4/3.

  5. Read off the 4th term of this ordered list: 336/420 = 4/5. Therefore the median of the data is 4/5.

Cross-check

Converting each value to a decimal reproduces exactly the same ranking, independently of the common-denominator method.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q44

text: The arithmetic mean of the observations 12, 46, 83, 43, 97, 34, 31, 33 and 26 is:
solution:
Concept: The arithmetic mean (average) of a set of n observations is the sum of all the observations divided by the number of observations: Mean = (Sum of all values) ÷ n.

Application:

  1. List the nine given observations: 12, 46, 83, 43, 97, 34, 31, 33, 26.

  2. Add the first five values: 12 + 46 + 83 + 43 + 97 = 281.

  3. Add the remaining four values: 34 + 31 + 33 + 26 = 124.

  4. Add the two partial sums to get the grand total: 281 + 124 = 405.

  5. Divide the grand total by the number of observations, 9: 405 ÷ 9 = 45.

Cross-check:

Subtracting 45 from each of the nine observations gives the deviations -33, 1, 38, -2, 52, -11, -14, -12 and -19. Adding these deviations gives exactly 0, confirming 45 is the mean, since the deviations of all observations from their true mean always sum to zero.

title: What is the median of data if its mode is
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Mean, Median, and Mode for grouped data
text: What is the median of data if its mode is 15 and the mean is 30?
solution:
To find the median when the mean and mode are known, we use the empirical relationship formula: 3 × Median = 2 × Mean + Mode.

Substitute the given values: Mode = 15 and Mean = 30.

Calculate: 3 × Median = 2(30) + 15

Simplify: 3 × Median = 60 + 15 = 75

Solve for Median: Median = 75 / 3 = 25.
