title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q99
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: A man sells two T.V.s at the same rate. In case of first T.V. he makes 10% profit and in case of second one he loses 10%. Then his loss or gain percent is
solution:
Concept: When an article is sold at the same selling price once at x% profit and once at x% loss, the two transactions never cancel out — the overall result is always a loss equal to (x/10)2 percent of the combined cost price, regardless of the actual selling price used.

Application: Let the common selling price of each T.V. be SP.

  1. For the first T.V., a 10% profit means SP = CP1 × 1.10, so CP1 = SP / 1.10 = 10·SP/11.

  2. For the second T.V., a 10% loss means SP = CP2 × 0.90, so CP2 = SP / 0.90 = 10·SP/9.

  3. Total cost price = CP1 + CP2 = 10·SP/11 + 10·SP/9 = SP × (90 + 110)/99 = 200·SP/99.

  4. Total selling price = SP + SP = 2·SP = 198·SP/99.

  5. Since total CP (200·SP/99) is greater than total SP (198·SP/99), the deal produces a net loss = 200·SP/99 − 198·SP/99 = 2·SP/99.

  6. Loss% = (Loss / Total CP) × 100 = (2·SP/99) ÷ (200·SP/99) × 100 = 1%.

Cross-check: Using the shortcut identity for equal-selling-price profit/loss pairs, loss% = (x/10)2 with x = 10 gives (10/10)2 = 12 = 1%, confirming the step-by-step result independently.

Result: The overall transaction is a net loss of 1%.

title: Dealer marked the price of an item above the cost
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Discount, Marked Price and Trader Tricks (Including False Weight)
text: A dealer marked the price of an item 40% above the cost price. He then gave successive discounts of 20% and 25% to a particular customer, resulting in a loss of ₹720. At what price did he sell the item to the customer?
solution:
Concept

A markup and a discount are percentages of different bases: the markup is taken on the cost price, while each discount is taken on the price standing just before it. So the chain is multiplicative — SP = CP × (1 + markup) × (1 − d1) × (1 − d2) — and the loss is simply CP − SP. Since every percentage factor is known, one unknown cost price can be recovered from the given loss amount.

Applying it here

  1. Let the cost price be ₹x. A markup of 40% above cost gives the marked price MP = 1.40x.

  2. The first discount of 20% leaves 80% of the marked price: 1.40x × 0.80 = 1.12x.

  3. The second discount of 25% is taken on that reduced price and leaves 75% of it: 1.12x × 0.75 = 0.84x. So SP = 0.84x.

  4. Loss = CP − SP = x − 0.84x = 0.16x.

  5. The loss is given as ₹720, so 0.16x = 720, which gives x = 720 ÷ 0.16 = ₹4,500 as the cost price.

  6. Therefore the selling price is SP = 0.84 × 4,500 = ₹3,780.

Cross-check

Rebuild the whole chain from a cost price of ₹4,500 and confirm that the loss comes back to ₹720:

Marked price = CP + 40%

After the further 25% discount (SP)

Loss = CP − SP

Note the trap: discounts of 20% and 25% are not a single 45% discount. Their combined effect is 1 − (0.80 × 0.75) = 0.40, i.e. 40% off. Even so, a 40% markup followed by 40% off ends in a loss, because the 40% is taken off the larger marked price while the 40% was added to the smaller cost price.

title: Dealer offers cash discount of and still makes profit of

text: A dealer offers a cash discount of 20% and still makes a profit of 20% when he further allows 16 articles to a dozen to a particularly sticky bargainer. By what percent above the cost price were his articles listed?
solution:
Let the cost price of one article be Rs. 1, and let the marked (listed) price of one article be Rs. M.

The deal has two layers. First, the dealer gives a 20% cash discount on the marked price. Second, "16 articles to a dozen" means the bargainer pays for a dozen (12 articles) but actually receives 16 articles.

Money the dealer receives = price charged for 12 articles after the 20% discount = 12 x M x (1 - 0.20) = 12 x 0.8 x M = 9.6M.

Goods the dealer hands over = 16 articles, costing 16 x 1 = Rs. 16.

He still makes a 20% profit, so his receipts equal 120% of his cost: 9.6M = 1.20 x 16 = 19.2.

Therefore M = 19.2 / 9.6 = 2. The marked price is Rs. 2 against a cost price of Rs. 1, i.e. twice the cost price.

So the articles were listed 100% above the cost price.

title: The successive discounts of and are equal to single discount
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Discount, Marked Price and Trader Tricks (Including False Weight)
text: The successive discounts of 20% and 15% are equal to a single discount of
solution:
For two successive percentage discounts applied one after another, the second discount is taken off the price that has already been reduced by the first discount, not off the original price. If the first rate is r1% and the second is r2%, the single discount that has the same overall effect is r1 + r2 − (r1 × r2)/100 — equivalently, the fraction of the original price left after both discounts equals (1 − r1/100) × (1 − r2/100).

  1. Take the original price as 100 (any convenient base works, since a percentage discount is scale-independent).

  2. Apply the first 20% discount: the price becomes 100 × (1 − 20/100) = 100 × 0.80 = 80.

  3. Apply the second 15% discount on this already-reduced price of 80 (not on the original 100): the price becomes 80 × (1 − 15/100) = 80 × 0.85 = 68.

  4. The total amount removed from the original price is 100 − 68 = 32 out of 100, so the single discount that has the same effect as the two successive discounts is 32%.

Cross-check with the direct successive-discount formula: combined discount = r1 + r2 − (r1 × r2)/100 = 20 + 15 − (20 × 15)/100 = 35 − 3 = 32%, which matches the step-by-step computation above.

optionFeedback.html: This adds the two discount rates directly (20 + 15) as a flat combined percentage.
This combines the two rates as successive INCREASES — (1.20) × (1.15) — rather than as decreases.

Successive discounts compound on the reduced price: (0.80) × (0.85) = 0.68 of the original price remains, so 32% has been removed — the single discount with the same overall effect as the two applied in sequence.
This treats the situation as though an extra small discount were being layered in beyond the two stated in the question.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q100
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Discount, Marked Price and Trader Tricks (Including False Weight)
text: A book seller gives discount successively at the rate 25% and 16% on a book. By selling the book, he gets Rs. 63. What is the actual price of the book?
solution:
CONCEPT: When two discounts are applied successively (one after the other), the final price is not the marked price reduced by the simple sum of the two percentages. Each discount acts on the price left after the previous discount, so the overall retained fraction of the marked price is the PRODUCT of the two individual retained fractions: retained fraction = (1 − first discount/100) × (1 − second discount/100).

Applying this to the question:

  1. Let the actual (marked) price of the book be P.

  2. After the first successive discount of 25%, the retained price is P × (1 − 25/100) = 0.75P.

  3. The second successive discount of 16% is applied to this already-reduced price (not to the original price P): 0.75P × (1 − 16/100) = 0.75P × 0.84 = 0.63P.

  4. This final amount equals the selling price stated in the question: 0.63P = Rs. 63.

  5. Solving for P: P = 63 ÷ 0.63 = Rs. 100.

CROSS-CHECK: Apply the two discounts forward on Rs. 100 to confirm. A 25% discount on Rs. 100 leaves Rs. 75. A further 16% discount on Rs. 75 removes Rs. 12, leaving Rs. 63 — which matches the selling price given in the question, confirming the result.

So the actual (marked) price of the book is Rs. 100.

Rs. 250 is exactly ten times the first discount rate of 25% stated in the question — a value a solver might reach by mistaking that rate for a rupee figure and scaling it directly into a price, rather than computing the marked price through the successive-discount method.

Rs. 630 is exactly ten times the selling price of Rs. 63 stated in the question — a value a solver might reach by misplacing the decimal point in the given selling price, rather than computing the marked price through the successive-discount method.

Rs. 1600 is a hundredfold multiple of the second discount rate of 16% stated in the question — a value a solver might reach by mistaking that rate for a rupee figure and scaling it directly into a price, rather than computing the marked price through the successive-discount method.

text: The list price of an article is ₹44000 and a discount of 10% is offered on the list price. What additional discount per cent on the already discounted price must be offered to a customer to bring the net selling price to ₹792?
solution:
Concept

Sequential discounts are applied one after another to the current price, not independently to the original price.

For a price P and a discount d%, the new price is P(1 − d/100). A second discount x% multiplies the already discounted price by (1 − x/100).

Application

  1. After the first 10% discount, the price is ₹44,000 × (1 − 10/100) = ₹44,000 × 0.90 = ₹39,600.

  2. Let x% be the additional discount. The required net price gives ₹39,600 × (1 − x/100) = ₹792.

  3. Divide by ₹39,600: 1 − x/100 = 792/39,600 = 0.02. Hence x/100 = 0.98, so x = 98.

Cross-check

An additional 98% discount leaves 2% of ₹39,600, and ₹39,600 × 0.02 = ₹792, which reproduces the required net selling price.

Therefore, the required additional discount is 98%.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q51

text: If an item marked at ₹8,100 is sold for ₹810, what is the discount percentage?
solution:
Concept

Discount percentage measures how much the marked price (MP) is reduced to reach the selling price (SP): Discount % = ((MP − SP) ÷ MP) × 100. Equivalently, SP = MP − Discount amount, so a larger discount percentage corresponds to a smaller selling price relative to the marked price.

  4. 7,290 ÷ 8,100 = 0.9, so Discount % = 0.9 × 100 = 90%.

solution:
Given:
5(√5)^(x+5) = (√5)^(2x+7)

Write 5 as:
5 = (√5)²

So,
(√5)² × (√5)^(x+5) = (√5)^(2x+7)

Using the law:
aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ

title: Find the sum of digits of product TCS This test

text: Find the sum of the digits of the product 16100 × 125135.
solution:
Concept: For numbers expressed as prime powers, (am)n = amn, and when two bases multiply to a round number such as 2 × 5 = 10, grouping (2a × 5a) = 10a turns a product into a power of ten times whatever factor is left over. Multiplying by 10a only appends a zeros to that leftover factor's digits, so the digit sum of the whole product equals the digit sum of the leftover factor alone.

  1. Write 16 as a power of 2: 16 = 24, so 16100 = (24)100 = 2400.

  2. Write 125 as a power of 5: 125 = 53, so 125135 = (53)135 = 5405.

  3. Multiply the two results, pairing as many 5's with 2's as possible: 2400 × 5405 = 2400 × 5400 × 55 = (2 × 5)400 × 55 = 10400 × 55.

  4. Evaluate the leftover factor: 55 = 54 × 5 = 625 × 5 = 3125.

  5. So the product equals 3125 followed by 400 zeros; every digit besides that leading '3125' block is 0, so the digit sum of the whole number is just the digit sum of 3125: 3 + 1 + 2 + 5 = 11.

Cross-check: 55 = 3125 can be verified directly (52 = 25, 53 = 125, 54 = 625, 55 = 3125), and re-adding its digits (3 + 1 + 2 + 5) confirms 11 independently of the exponent manipulation above.

optionFeedback.html: This equals the digit sum of 235 (100 + 135) — the result of adding the original exponents of 16 and 125 as though they shared one common base. Exponents add only when the base is the same, and 16 and 125 are different bases, so this total has no real connection to the product's value.

Once 16100 and 125135 are each rewritten as a power of a single prime and fully combined, the product reduces to 3125 followed only by zeros — and the digit sum of 3125 is 3 + 1 + 2 + 5 = 11, which is exactly this value.

This equals the digit sum of 805 — a number that would only appear if you summed two intermediate exponents produced partway through converting the two bases into prime powers, instead of fully evaluating what those powers multiply out to. Exponents are not the number itself, and combining them this way isn't a valid step in simplifying the expression.

This does not match the digit sum obtained once each base is correctly rewritten as a power of its own prime and the two results are fully combined — recompute that combination from scratch rather than adjusting a partial or estimated figure.

Idea: de-nest each radical using the identities x + y − 2√(xy) = (√x − √y)² and x + y + 2√(xy) = (√x + √y)².

text: The average of 7 numbers is 29. The average of first three of them is 23 and the last three of them is 42. Then the fourth number is:
solution:
Concept

The average of a set of numbers equals their total sum divided by how many numbers there are, so Sum = Average × Count. When the same numbers are split into overlapping or adjacent groups, the sum of every individual number must still add up to the one grand total — a missing term is found by subtracting all the known partial sums from that total.

Application

  1. Total of all 7 numbers = 29 × 7 = 203.

  2. Sum of the first three numbers = 23 × 3 = 69.

  3. Sum of the last three numbers = 42 × 3 = 126.

  4. The first three, the fourth number, and the last three together make all seven, so: 69 + (fourth) + 126 = 203.

  5. 69 + 126 = 195, therefore fourth = 203 − 195 = 8.

Cross-check

Add the parts back: 69 + 8 + 126 = 203, which equals 29 × 7. The grand total is reproduced exactly, so the fourth number is 8.

text: The average of 5 consecutive integers starting with m is n. What is the average of 6 consecutive integers starting with (m+2)?
solution:
To determine the average of 6 consecutive integers starting with (m + 2), let's break down the problem systematically.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Analyze the first sequence:

The 5 consecutive integers starting with m are: m, (m + 1), (m + 2), (m + 3), (m + 4).

The average of these integers is the middle term, which is (m + 2).

Given that this average is n, we establish the relationship: n = m + 2.

Analyze the second sequence:

The 6 consecutive integers starting with (m + 2) are: (m + 2), (m + 3), (m + 4), (m + 5), (m + 6), (m + 7).

The sum of these 6 integers is: 6m + (2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7) = 6m + 27.

The average is the sum divided by the count: (6m + 27) / 6 = m + 4.5.

Express the new average in terms of n:

We know from Step 1 that m = n - 2.

Substitute this into the average expression from Step 2: (n - 2) + 4.5 = n + 2.5.

Convert n + 2.5 into a fraction: (2n + 5) / 2.

Correct Option
Option A: (2n+5)/2

text: The average weight of a class of 29 students is 40 kgs. If the weight of the teacher be included, the average rises by 500 grams. What is the weight of the teacher?

text:

solution:
The average (mean) of a group of numbers is (sum of all the numbers) divided by (how many numbers there are). Because of this definition, a fixed rule holds: if the same amount is added to, or subtracted from, every single number in a group, the average changes by exactly that same amount, since the total sum changes by (count of numbers x that amount), and dividing by the count leaves the change unchanged.

  1. The average of 7 numbers is given as 49, so their total sum = 7 x 49 = 343.

  3. New sum = 343 - 28 = 315.

  4. New average = new sum / count = 315 / 7 = 45.

Cross-check using the rule directly: new average = old average - (amount subtracted from each number) = 49 - 4 = 45, which matches the sum-based calculation above.

So the new average is 45.

text: In a class of 60 students, 60% are girls. The average weight of the boys is 62 kg and that of the girls is 58 kg. What is the average weight (in kg) of the whole class?
solution:
Given:

  • Total students = 60

  • Girls = 60% of the class

  • Boys = the remaining students

  • Average weight of boys = 62 kg

  • Average weight of girls = 58 kg

Step 1: Find the number of boys and girls

Girls = 60% of 60
= (60/100) × 60
= 36
Boys = 60 − 36
= 24

Step 2: Find the total weight of boys and girls

Total weight of boys = 24 × 62 = 1488 kg
Total weight of girls = 36 × 58 = 2088 kg

Step 3: Find the average weight of the whole class

Total weight of the class = 1488 + 2088 = 3576 kg
Average weight = Total weight ÷ Total students
= 3576 ÷ 60
= 59.6 kg

Hence, the average weight of the whole class is 59.6 kg.

text: The average of 7 numbers is 30. The average of the first three of them is 23 and the last three of them is 42. Then the fourth number is:
solution:
Concept

The sum of a set of numbers equals its average multiplied by how many numbers there are (Sum = Average x Count). When a whole group is split into adjoining sub-groups, a single missing value can be recovered by subtracting the sub-group sums from the total sum.

Application

Seven numbers are split as: the first three, the single fourth number, and the last three. Compute each known sum, then isolate the fourth:

  1. Total of all 7 numbers = 30 x 7 = 210.

  2. Sum of the first three = 23 x 3 = 69.

  3. Sum of the last three = 42 x 3 = 126.

  4. Fourth number = Total - (first three) - (last three) = 210 - 69 - 126 = 15.

Cross-check

Add the parts back: 69 (first three) + 15 (fourth) + 126 (last three) = 210, and 210 / 7 = 30, which matches the given overall average. So the fourth number is 15.

25 typically appears when the two given sub-group averages are blended directly -- treating the missing number as some rough combination of 23 and 42 -- instead of converting each average into its own sum first. A value found by blending averages this way is not required to satisfy the overall average of 30, so it is an estimate rather than a value consistent with every condition given.

20 typically appears from a count mistake in how the numbers are split -- for instance treating the group left over after the first three and last three as bigger than a single number -- which changes how much of the overall total is left to assign to the missing value. That shifted leftover no longer matches the number that keeps all three stated averages true together.

10 typically appears when one sub-group's contribution is counted twice -- for instance treating the fourth number as already included inside the first-three or last-three total before subtracting it out separately. Double-counting a group like this pulls the leftover value down below the number that actually satisfies the stated averages.

text: Average weight of boys in a class is 55 kg while average weight of girls in the same class is 35 kg. If the average of all the students in the class is 40 kg, find the ratio of boys and girls in the class.
solution:
Concept

When two groups are combined, the overall (weighted) average lies between the two group averages. The rule of alligation states that the two groups split in the inverse ratio of their distances from the overall average:

(number in group 1) : (number in group 2) = (distance of group 2's average from the mean) : (distance of group 1's average from the mean).

Application

  1. Boys' average = 55 kg, girls' average = 35 kg, overall average = 40 kg. Let the number of boys be b and girls be g.

  2. Total weight equation: 55b + 35g = 40(b + g).

  3. Expand the right side: 55b + 35g = 40b + 40g.

  4. Collect like terms: 55b − 40b = 40g − 35g, so 15b = 5g.

  5. Divide both sides by 5: 3b = g, hence b : g = 1 : 3.

Cross-check (alligation)

Distance of boys' average from the mean = 55 − 40 = 15; distance of girls' average from the mean = 40 − 35 = 5. By alligation, boys : girls = 5 : 15 = 1 : 3, which matches.

So boys : girls = 1 : 3.

optionFeedback.html: This inverts which group is larger. Since the overall average of 40 kg is much closer to the girls' 35 kg than to the boys' 55 kg, the heavier-averaging group (boys) cannot be the larger one.

This treats the two groups as nearly balanced, which would pull the overall average toward the midpoint of 55 and 35 (i.e. 45 kg). The given average is 40 kg, well below that midpoint, so the groups are not close to this ratio.
With 1 part boys to 3 parts girls, the combined average is (55·1 + 35·3) / (1 + 3) = (55 + 105) / 4 = 160 / 4 = 40 kg, exactly the stated class average.
This makes boys the larger group, but a class average of 40 kg lies nearer the girls' 35 kg than the boys' 55 kg, so the group closer to the mean must be the more numerous one.

title: How many real solutions does the equation x7+14x5+16x3+30x−560=0 have?
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: How many real solutions does the equation x7 + 14x5 + 16x3 + 30x − 560 = 0 have?
solution:
Concept

A continuous function has at least one real zero when its values change sign. A function whose derivative is positive everywhere is strictly increasing, so it can have at most one real zero.

For an odd-degree polynomial with positive leading coefficient, the value tends to −∞ as x tends to −∞ and to +∞ as x tends to +∞.

Application

  1. Define f(x) = x7 + 14x5 + 16x3 + 30x − 560. This polynomial is continuous for every real x.

  2. Differentiate: f′(x) = 7x6 + 70x4 + 48x2 + 30.

  3. For every real x, the even powers x6, x4, and x2 are non-negative. Therefore f′(x) ≥ 30 > 0, so f is strictly increasing and can cross zero at most once.

  4. Because f(x) tends to −∞ as x tends to −∞ and to +∞ as x tends to +∞, continuity guarantees at least one real zero.

Cross-check

Direct values bracket a zero: f(1) = −499 < 0, while f(2) = 204 > 0. Thus a real zero lies between 1 and 2; strict increase prevents any second zero.

Therefore, the equation has exactly 1 real solution.

text: If x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = 527, then the value of x + 1/x is
solution:
Concept

For any nonzero x, the symmetric powers are linked by repeated squaring of the basic sum s = x + 1/x. Squaring a sum adds the cross term, so (a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2. With b = 1/a the middle term is the constant 2, which lets each higher power be reached from the one below.

Application

  1. Let s = x + 1/x. Squaring: s2 = x2 + 2 + 1/x2, so x2 + 1/x2 = s2 - 2.

  2. Square again: (x2 + 1/x2)2 = x4 + 2 + 1/x4, so x4 + 1/x4 = (x2 + 1/x2)2 - 2.

  3. Substitute: 527 = (x2 + 1/x2)2 - 2, so (x2 + 1/x2)2 = 529 and x2 + 1/x2 = ±23.

  4. For real x, x2 + 1/x2 ≥ 2 (a square plus its reciprocal is always at least 2 by AM-GM), so the -23 branch is impossible and x2 + 1/x2 = 23.

  5. Back to step 1: s2 - 2 = 23, so s2 = 25 and s = x + 1/x = ±5.

s2 = 25 admits both +5 and -5 (for real x, +5 corresponds to x > 0 and -5 to x < 0). Only positive values are offered here, so the answer is 5, matching the standard convention of taking the positive root for this problem type.

Forward from s = 5: x2 + 1/x2 = 52 - 2 = 23, and x4 + 1/x4 = 232 - 2 = 527, matching the given value (s = -5 gives the same fourth power, since only even powers appear).

title: Which among the following can be expressed as where and

text: Which among the following can be expressed as (10p + q) (10q + p), where p and q are integers?
solution:
For any integers p and q — not necessarily single digits — let a = 10p + q and b = 10q + p; b swaps the coefficients of p and q, the same pattern as reversing a two-digit number's digits when p, q happen to be 0-9. The product expands algebraically to (10p + q)(10q + p) = 10p2 + 101pq + 10q2. Since a + b = 11(p + q) and a − b = 9(p − q), a target number N is expressible in this form ONLY IF N has some factor pair (a, b) — checked across ALL its divisor pairs, not only ones that look like two-digit reversals — whose sum is a multiple of 11 AND whose difference is a multiple of 9; p and q are then recovered as p = (10a − b) / 99 and q = (10b − a) / 99.

  1. Check 1207: its factor pair 17 × 71 gives sum 17 + 71 = 88 = 11 × 8 (a multiple of 11) and difference 71 − 17 = 54 = 9 × 6 (a multiple of 9) — both required conditions hold.

  2. Recover p and q from a = 17, b = 71: p = (10a − b) / 99 = (170 − 71) / 99 = 1 and q = (10b − a) / 99 = (710 − 17) / 99 = 7, both integers.

  3. So p = 1, q = 7 gives 10p + q = 17 and 10q + p = 71, and 17 × 71 = 1207 exactly — the required form is satisfied.

  4. Checking every divisor pair of the other three values the same way: for 1344, three pairs have a sum divisible by 11 — (3, 448) with sum 451, (8, 168) with sum 176, and (14, 96) with sum 110 — but none of their differences (445, 160, and 82) is divisible by 9; for 1728 and 1296, no divisor pair at all has a sum divisible by 11. So none of 1344, 1728, or 1296 has any factor pair meeting both conditions, for any integers p and q — not only when p, q are restricted to single digits.

Cross-check by substituting p = 1 and q = 7 directly into the expansion: 10p2 + 101pq + 10q2 = 10(1) + 101(7) + 10(49) = 10 + 707 + 490 = 1207, matching independently.

So 1207 is the only one of the four values expressible as (10p + q)(10q + p) for integers p and q.

Why do we choose F(x)? The equation whose root we need is ax² + bx + c = 0. Rolle’s theorem gives a zero of a derivative, so we deliberately construct a function F(x) whose derivative is this quadratic.

title: If two is added to the denominator of rational number
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If two is added to the denominator of a rational number it becomes 1/3 and if 4 is added to the numerator it becomes 1/2. Then the sum of the numerator and the denominator of the rational number is:
solution:
Concept

A statement "a fraction becomes 1/k when something is changed" is an equation between two fractions. Cross-multiply each such statement to turn it into a linear equation, then solve the resulting system (here by elimination) for the unknown numerator and denominator.

Application

Let the rational number be x/y, where x is the numerator and y the denominator.

  1. First condition: adding 2 to the denominator gives 1/3, so x/(y+2) = 1/3. Cross-multiplying: 3x = y + 2, i.e. 3x − y = 2.

  2. Second condition: adding 4 to the numerator gives 1/2, so (x+4)/y = 1/2. Cross-multiplying: 2(x+4) = y, i.e. 2x − y = −8.

  3. Eliminate y by subtracting the second equation from the first: (3x − y) − (2x − y) = 2 − (−8), which gives x = 10.

  4. Substitute x = 10 into 3x − y = 2: 30 − y = 2, so y = 28.

  5. The required sum is x + y = 10 + 28 = 38.

Cross-check

Verify both conditions with x = 10, y = 28: x/(y+2) = 10/30 = 1/3 ✓ and (x+4)/y = 14/28 = 1/2 ✓. Both hold, so the numerator-plus-denominator sum is 38.

title: If two is added to the denominator of rational number
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If two is added to the denominator of a rational number it becomes 1 and if 4 is added to the numerator it becomes 1/2. Then the sum of the numerator and the denominator of the rational number is:
solution:
Concept

A rational number is a fraction numerator/denominator. When a worded condition says a fraction "becomes" a value after changing its numerator or denominator, translate each statement into a linear equation and solve the resulting system by substitution.

Application

Let the rational number be N/D, where N is the numerator and D is the denominator.

  1. Adding 2 to the denominator makes the fraction equal to 1: N / (D + 2) = 1, so N = D + 2.

  2. Adding 4 to the numerator makes the fraction equal to 1/2: (N + 4) / D = 1/2, so 2(N + 4) = D, that is 2N + 8 = D.

  3. Substitute N = D + 2 into 2N + 8 = D: 2(D + 2) + 8 = D, giving 2D + 4 + 8 = D.

  4. Simplify: 2D + 12 = D, so D = -12, and then N = D + 2 = -10.

  5. Required sum = N + D = -10 + (-12) = -22.

Cross-check

With N = -10 and D = -12 the fraction is -10/-12 = 5/6. Verify: N/(D+2) = -10/-10 = 1 and (N+4)/D = -6/-12 = 1/2. Both conditions hold, so the sum -22 is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Solving the two conditions together gives the numerator and denominator whose sum is exactly this, so this value is right.
This results from subtracting the numerator and denominator in the wrong order; the question asks for their sum, not a signed difference.
This results from taking the difference of the numerator and denominator instead of adding them; re-read the question, which asks for the sum.
This comes from solving for the values but then ignoring the signs that the two equations produce and adding the bare magnitudes; the signs must be carried through to the sum.

text: If 2 is added to the denominator of a rational number, it becomes 1/2 and if 34 is added to the numerator it becomes 1/4 . Then the sum of the numerator and the denominator of the rational number is:
solution:
Concept

A rational number is written as a fraction numerator/denominator. When a condition says the fraction equals a target value after a change, translate it into an equation by cross-multiplication: a/b = p/q means a*q = b*p. Two independent conditions give two linear equations, which are solved simultaneously for the numerator and the denominator.

Application

Let the numerator be N and the denominator be D, so the number is N/D.

  1. Condition 1 - adding 2 to the denominator gives 1/2: N/(D + 2) = 1/2. Cross-multiply: 2N = D + 2, so D = 2N - 2.

  2. Condition 2 - adding 34 to the numerator gives 1/4: (N + 34)/D = 1/4. Cross-multiply: 4(N + 34) = D, so D = 4N + 136.

  3. Equate the two expressions for D: 2N - 2 = 4N + 136, which gives -2N = 138, so N = -69.

  4. Substitute back: D = 2(-69) - 2 = -140.

  5. Required sum = N + D = -69 + (-140) = -209.

Cross-check

The number is -69/-140 = 69/140. Add 2 to the denominator: -69/(-138) = 69/138 = 1/2. Add 34 to the numerator: (-69 + 34)/-140 = -35/-140 = 35/140 = 1/4. Both conditions hold, so the sum is -209.

Substituting these numerator and denominator values back into both original conditions reproduces 1/2 and 1/4 exactly, so this total is consistent with the problem.

title: If the thrice of three consecutive odd no is equal
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If thrice the first of three consecutive odd numbers is equal to 3 more than twice the last number, then find the 3rd largest of these odd numbers.
solution:
Three consecutive odd numbers can be represented algebraically as x, x + 2, and x + 4, where x is the first (smallest) and x + 4 is the last (largest) of the three. To find a specific term such as the '3rd largest', first solve for x from the given condition, then rank the three resulting numbers from largest to smallest.

Applying this to the given condition:

  1. Let the three consecutive odd numbers be x, x + 2, and x + 4.

  2. The condition states thrice the first number equals 3 more than twice the last number: 3x = 2(x + 4) + 3.

  3. Expand the right-hand side: 3x = 2x + 8 + 3 = 2x + 11.

  4. Solve for x: 3x - 2x = 11, so x = 11.

  5. The three consecutive odd numbers are 11, 13, and 15.

  6. Ranking them from largest to smallest: 15 is the 1st largest, 13 is the 2nd largest, and 11 is the 3rd largest.

Cross-check: 3 × 11 = 33, and 2 × 15 + 3 = 33 — both sides match, confirming x = 11 is correct.

Hence, the 3rd largest of the three odd numbers is 11.

title: The sum of positive number and its reciprocal is twice
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: The sum of a positive number and its reciprocal is twice the difference of the number and its reciprocal. The number is:
solution:
Concept: To translate a word problem about the sum and difference of a number and its reciprocal into an equation, let the number be x, write the sum as x + 1/x and the difference as x − 1/x, translate the given relationship between the two into a single equation, and solve for x — keeping only the root(s) that satisfy any stated constraint such as positivity.

Application:

  1. Let the positive number be x, so its reciprocal is 1/x.

  2. The sum of the number and its reciprocal is x + 1/x, and their difference is x − 1/x.

  3. The problem states that the sum equals twice the difference: x + 1/x = 2(x − 1/x).

  4. Expand the right-hand side: x + 1/x = 2x − 2/x.

  5. Move the 1/x terms to the left and the x terms to the right: 1/x + 2/x = 2x − x.

  6. Combine like terms on each side: 3/x = x.

  7. Multiply both sides by x: 3 = x2.

  8. Since the number is positive, take the positive square root: x = √3.

Cross-check: With x = √3, the reciprocal 1/x = √3⁄3. Sum = √3 + √3⁄3 = 4√3⁄3, and difference = √3 − √3⁄3 = 2√3⁄3, so twice the difference = 4√3⁄3 — equal to the sum, confirming the value.

Result: The number is √3.

optionFeedback.html: This is what results if the difference is set up in reverse order — using (reciprocal − number) instead of (number − reciprocal) in the sum-equals-twice-the-difference equation. That reversed order changes the sign of a key term and leads to this value instead of the number that actually satisfies the condition as stated.

This value follows if, after combining the 1/x terms to reach 3/x on the left, the x term on the right is not fully accounted for — the equation is left as 3/x = 2x instead of subtracting x from that side — which doubles a key coefficient and produces this value rather than the number that actually fits the problem's condition.

Writing the sum as x + 1/x and the difference as x − 1/x, and setting the sum equal to twice the difference, gives 3/x = x, so x2 = 3. Since the number is stated to be positive, this positive square root is exactly the value that satisfies the condition.

This follows if a term is dropped while rearranging the equation, changing a key coefficient and leaving 2/x = x, which gives x2 = 2; reporting the reciprocal of that intermediate result instead of the number itself produces this value.

title: Directions Solve the quadratic and answer the following questions. One
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text:
Directions: Solve the quadratic equations and answer the question that follows.

A: (x − 2)2 = −3x2 + 22 + 25x − P
B: (10y2 − 32y + 2/3) × 3 + 10y = 0

One root of equation A is 5.

Which of the following are the roots of equation B?
solution:
Concept

A quadratic in the form ay2 + by + c = 0 is solved by first reducing the given expression to this standard form, then factorising the middle term (split b into two parts whose product is a·c and whose sum is b). The two factors give the two roots. Always simplify every bracket and multiplier before reading off a, b and c.

Application — Equation B

  1. Expand the inner bracket times 3: (10y2 − 9y + 2/3) × 3 = 30y2 − 27y + 2. (Note 32 = 9 and (2/3)×3 = 2.)

  2. Add the remaining 10y: 30y2 − 27y + 2 + 10y = 30y2 − 17y + 2 = 0. So a = 30, b = −17, c = 2.

  3. Split the middle term using a·c = 30 × 2 = 60 and sum = −17: the parts are −12 and −5 (since −12 × −5 = 60 and −12 + −5 = −17).

  4. Factorise: 30y2 − 12y − 5y + 2 = 6y(5y − 2) − 1(5y − 2) = (5y − 2)(6y − 1) = 0.

  5. Set each factor to zero: 5y − 2 = 0 → y = 2/5; 6y − 1 = 0 → y = 1/6.

Roots of equation B: 2/5 and 1/6.

Cross-check

Sum of roots should equal −b/a = 17/30. Check: 2/5 + 1/6 = 12/30 + 5/30 = 17/30. ✓ Product should equal c/a = 2/30 = 1/15. Check: (2/5)(1/6) = 2/30 = 1/15. ✓ Both match, confirming the roots.

optionFeedback.html: This pair results from carrying the wrong constant term after the whole inner bracket is multiplied by 3. Re-multiply every term inside the bracket — including the fraction — by 3 before forming the standard quadratic, and the smaller root changes. The slip lies in the multiplication step, not the factorising.

The 1/3 here comes from leaving the squared coefficient unsquared — reading 32y as a first-power term. Evaluate the exponent before collecting like terms; once it is squared the middle coefficient shifts and this pairing no longer factorises cleanly.

These are the values that satisfy equation B: substituting each back makes the reduced quadratic vanish, and they reproduce the correct sum and product of roots for that quadratic. This is the complete and consistent root pair.

Pairs like 2/3 and 3/5 come from guessing denominators that are not consistent with how the leading coefficient factors. A root's denominator must divide the leading coefficient; test each candidate by substitution and 2/3 and 3/5 do not zero the equation.

Equation B has a non-negative discriminant and two real rational roots, and one of the listed numeric pairs satisfies it on substitution. "None of the above" is justified only when no listed pair works — substitution shows that is not the situation here.

title: In each of these questions, two equation and (II) are
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text:
In each of these questions, two equation (I) and (II) are given. You have to solve both the equations and give answer.

I. 4x² + 20x + 25 = 0
II. 2y² + 11y + 15 = 0

options.html: If x = y or no relation can be established between x and y

solution:
Concept

To compare two variables that are each defined by a separate quadratic equation, solve each equation on its own to get its roots, then compare every root of the first variable against every root of the second. A single overall relation (≥, ≤, >, < or =) holds only when it is true for all such pairings; if some pairs give one sign and others give equality or the opposite sign, the relation must be widened or declared indeterminate. A perfect-square quadratic gives one repeated root.

Application

  1. Equation I: 4x2 + 20x + 25 = 0 is a perfect square, since it equals (2x + 5)2 = 0. So 2x + 5 = 0, giving the single repeated root x = −5/2 = −2.5.

  2. Equation II: 2y2 + 11y + 15 = 0. Factor by splitting the middle term: 2y2 + 6y + 5y + 15 = 2y(y + 3) + 5(y + 3) = (2y + 5)(y + 3) = 0. So y = −5/2 = −2.5 or y = −3.

  3. Compare x = −2.5 with each y value: against y = −2.5 we get x = y; against y = −3 we get −2.5 > −3, i.e. x > y.

  4. Across both cases x is never less than y — it is either equal to y or greater than y — so the relation that holds for every pair is x ≥ y.

Cross-check

Place the values on a number line: x sits at −2.5, while y is at −2.5 or −3. The smallest y (−3) lies to the left of x, and the largest y (−2.5) coincides with x. There is no y to the right of x, so x can never be strictly less than y; the tightest single relation covering both equal and greater cases is x ≥ y.

optionFeedback.html: This treats x as strictly greater than y in every case, but one root of the second equation is y = −2.5, which is exactly equal to x = −2.5. Because equality occurs for that pairing, a strict “greater than” cannot hold for all pairs.
With x = −2.5 and y ∈ {−2.5, −3}, x equals y in one pairing and exceeds y in the other, so x is never below y. The single relation that covers both the equal and the greater case is x ≥ y.

Choosing “less than” means x should sit to the left of y on the number line. But x = −2.5 coincides with one y value (−2.5) and lies to the right of the other (−3), so it is to the left of neither. The strict “x < y” claim therefore matches neither root pairing.
This would require x to be at most y in every case, but for y = −3 we have x = −2.5, which lies to the right of −3, so x exceeds y there. A “less than or equal” relation therefore fails.

Equality is not the only outcome — it holds only when y = −2.5; for y = −3, x = −2.5 is larger. A consistent one-directional relation does exist across both cases, so this is not a “no relation” situation.

subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If x1​ and x2​ are the roots of the equation 2x2+3x−9=0 then the equation which has the roots 1/x1​ and 1/x2 is:
solution:
Concept

For a quadratic ax2+bx+c=0 with roots α and β, Vieta's formulas give the sum α+β = −b/a and the product αβ = c/a. To build a new quadratic whose roots are expressions of α and β, first compute the new sum S and new product P, then write x2 − Sx + P = 0.

Reciprocal-root shortcut: replacing x with 1/x in ax2+bx+c=0 (i.e. reversing the order of the coefficients) yields the equation whose roots are 1/α and 1/β, namely cx2+bx+a=0.

Application

  1. Here a=2, b=3, c=−9, so the original roots satisfy x1+x2 = −b/a = −3/2 and x1x2 = c/a = −9/2.

  2. New sum: 1/x1 + 1/x2 = (x1+x2)/(x1x2) = (−3/2)/(−9/2) = 1/3.

  3. New product: 1/(x1x2) = 1/(−9/2) = −2/9.

  4. Form the equation: x2 − (1/3)x + (−2/9) = 0, i.e. x2 − (1/3)x − 2/9 = 0.

  5. Multiply through by 9 to clear the denominators: 9x2 − 3x − 2 = 0.

Cross-check

Apply the reciprocal shortcut directly: substitute x → 1/x in 2x2+3x−9=0 to get 2/x2 + 3/x − 9 = 0; multiplying by x2 gives 2 + 3x − 9x2 = 0, and multiplying by −1 gives 9x2 − 3x − 2 = 0 — the same equation, confirming the result.

optionFeedback.html: A frequent error here is to mishandle a sign while computing the sum of the reciprocal roots 1/x1 + 1/x2 and substituting it into the equation. Recompute that sum from the exact values of x1+x2 and x1x2 before assembling the quadratic.

A quadratic and its negative share the same roots, so before testing it you must make the leading coefficient positive — and doing so flips the sign of every term. The equation you then obtain does not have the required reciprocal roots, so recompute in standard form from the sum and product of those roots.
These coefficients are exactly the ones the sum 1/3 and product −2/9 of the reciprocal roots produce once the denominator is cleared, so this equation has the required roots.
A common slip here is to mishandle the sign when taking the reciprocal of the product of the roots to form the constant term. Recompute x1x2 and carry its sign carefully through the reciprocal.

solution:
Concept

For a quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots p and q, the sum of roots is p + q = -b/a and the product is pq = c/a. To obtain the equation whose roots are the reciprocals 1/p and 1/q, note that their sum is (p + q)/(pq) and their product is 1/(pq); the required equation is then x² - (new sum)x + (new product) = 0.

Application

  1. From x² + 2x - 15 = 0, identify a = 1, b = 2, c = -15, so x₁ + x₂ = -b/a = -2 and x₁·x₂ = c/a = -15.

  2. Sum of the new roots: 1/x₁ + 1/x₂ = (x₁ + x₂)/(x₁·x₂) = (-2)/(-15) = 2/15.

  3. Product of the new roots: (1/x₁)(1/x₂) = 1/(x₁·x₂) = 1/(-15) = -1/15.

  4. Form the equation: x² - (2/15)x + (-1/15) = 0.

  5. Clear the denominator by multiplying every term by 15: 15x² - 2x - 1 = 0.

Their sum is -1/5 + 1/3 = 2/15 and their product is -1/15, which match the coefficients of 15x² - 2x - 1 = 0. Substituting x = 1/3 gives 15(1/9) - 2(1/3) - 1 = 5/3 - 2/3 - 1 = 0, confirming the result.

optionFeedback.html: With the new roots summing to 2/15 and multiplying to -1/15, scaling x² - (2/15)x - 1/15 = 0 by 15 gives exactly 15x² - 2x - 1 = 0, so this equation has 1/x₁ and 1/x₂ as its roots.

This form comes from treating the sum of the new roots, (x₁ + x₂)/(x₁·x₂), as a negative quantity. title: If 2x+2/x=3 then the value of is:

text: If 2x + (2/x) = 3, then the value of x³ + (1/x³) + 2 is:
solution:
Given: 2x + (2/x) = 3.

Divide both sides by 2: x + (1/x) = 3/2.

Rearranging: x³ + 1/x³ = (x + 1/x)³ - 3(x + 1/x) = (3/2)³ - 3(3/2).

Finally add 2: x³ + 1/x³ + 2 = -9/8 + 16/8 = 7/8.

Therefore the required value is 7/8.

title: Twenty times positive integer is less than its square by
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: Twenty times a positive integer is less than its square by 96. What is the integer?
solution:
Concept: A word problem translates into an equation phrase by phrase. "A is less than B by C" means B − A = C. Let the positive integer be x; "its square" is x2 and "twenty times" the integer is 20x, so the stated relation becomes the quadratic x2 − 20x = 96.

  1. Set up the equation: x2 − 20x = 96, i.e. x2 − 20x − 96 = 0.

  2. Factor the quadratic: find two numbers whose product is −96 and whose sum is −20 — these are −24 and 4, since (−24) × 4 = −96 and (−24) + 4 = −20.

  3. So x2 − 20x − 96 = (x − 24)(x + 4) = 0, giving x = 24 or x = −4.

  4. The problem restricts the integer to be positive, so reject x = −4 and keep x = 24.

Cross-check: 242 − 20 × 24 = 576 − 480 = 96, exactly the difference stated in the question, confirming the value.

title: If and then the minimum value of 2y−3x is:
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: If −5 ≤ x ≤ 3 and −1 ≤ y ≤ 0, then the minimum value of 2y − 3x is:
solution:
Concept: A linear expression in variables that vary independently over a rectangular (box) domain reaches its extreme values at the corner points, and each term can be optimised on its own. A term with a positive coefficient is made as small as possible by taking its variable at the low end of its interval; a term with a negative coefficient is made as small as possible by taking its variable at the high end.

  2. The term -3x has a negative coefficient, so it is smallest when x is at its highest value, x = 3, giving -3x = -9.

  3. Adding the two smallest contributions: f = (-2) + (-9) = -11.

Cross-check: At the corner (x, y) = (3, -1): 2(-1) - 3(3) = -2 - 9 = -11. The opposite corner (x, y) = (-5, 0) gives 2(0) - 3(-5) = 15, which is the maximum, so -11 is indeed the minimum.

title: Data driven machine is one that executes an instruction if

A data driven machine is one that executes an instruction if the needed data is available. The physical ordering of the code listing does not dictate the course of execution. Consider the following pseudo-code:

(B) Add A and B to get E

(C) Add B with 0.5 to get D

Instructions C and E rely on initial inputs and do not affect the dependency chain for G, but a valid sequence must ensure B precedes A, and both precede D.

text: If it takes two workers, working separately but at the same speed, 2 hours and 40 minutes to complete a particular task, about how long will it take one worker, working at the same speed, to complete the same task alone?
solution:
To solve this problem, we must understand the inverse relationship between the number of workers and the time required to complete a task.

Step-by-Step Analysis
Standardize Units: First, convert the given time into minutes for easier calculation.

2 hours and 40 minutes = (2 × 60) + 40 = 120 + 40 = 160 minutes.

Analyze the Work Relationship: The problem states two workers take 160 minutes working separately. This implies that if both workers were working simultaneously on the same task, the time would be shorter; however, the prompt clarifies they are working "separately but at the same speed" to complete a particular task. If the total man-hours required for the task is distributed among them, reducing the workforce to one worker means the remaining worker must perform the total work alone.

Calculate the Time for One Worker: Since one worker is doing the work that two workers were splitting, it will take twice as long.

Time = 160 minutes × 2 = 320 minutes.

Convert Back to Hours and Minutes:

320 minutes ÷ 60 minutes/hour = 5 hours with a remainder of 20 minutes.

Total time = 5 hours and 20 minutes.

Correct Option
Option D: 5 hrs. 20 min

text: A can finish the work in 30 days and B in 40 days. They both work together for 5 days and then B leaves. How many days will A take to complete the remaining work?
solution:
Concept

In work-rate problems, each worker's one-day output is the reciprocal of the time they take alone. Outputs add when people work together, the total job equals 1 (or, conveniently, the LCM of the individual times in "units"), and remaining time equals remaining work divided by the rate of whoever finishes it.

Application

  1. Take the total work as the LCM of 30 and 40, which is 120 units. Then A does 120/30 = 4 units per day and B does 120/40 = 3 units per day.

  2. Working together, their combined output is 4 + 3 = 7 units per day. Over 5 days they complete 7 x 5 = 35 units.

  3. Work still left after B leaves = 120 - 35 = 85 units.

  4. A finishes this alone at 4 units per day, so the time needed = 85 / 4 = 21.25 days.

Cross-check

Using fractions instead of units: in 5 days the pair completes 5 x (1/30 + 1/40) = 5 x 7/120 = 7/24 of the job, leaving 17/24. A alone needs (17/24) / (1/30) = (17/24) x 30 = 21.25 days, which matches.

title: Combined work rate with 8-hour workday

text: X can complete one work in 5 days. Y can complete the same work twice in 15 days, and Z can complete the same work three times in 7 days. If they work together for 8 hours a day, how much time will they take to complete one work?
solution:
CONCEPT: In time-and-work questions, each person's capacity is converted into a rate: work completed per day. When people work together, their rates are added; if a workday has fixed hours, fractional working days are converted into hours by multiplying by hours per day.

  1. X completes 1 work in 5 days, so X's rate is 1/5 work per day.

  2. Y completes 2 works in 15 days, so Y's rate is 2/15 work per day.

  3. Z completes 3 works in 7 days, so Z's rate is 3/7 work per day.

  4. Combined rate = 1/5 + 2/15 + 3/7 = 21/105 + 14/105 + 45/105 = 80/105 = 16/21 work per day.

  5. Time for 1 work = 1 divided by (16/21) = 21/16 working days.

  6. Each working day is 8 hours, so time = (21/16) × 8 = 21/2 hours = 10.5 hours.

CROSS-CHECK: In 10.5 working hours, the fraction of an 8-hour day is 10.5/8 = 21/16 days; multiplying this by the combined rate 16/21 gives exactly 1 full work.

Therefore, the required time is 10 hours 30 minutes.

X + Z = 1/45 - 1/180

Convert to common denominator: 4/180 - 1/180 = 3/180 = 1/60 per day.

Since X + Z complete 1/60 of the work in one day, they will take 60 days to complete the entire job.

solution:
Concept

Efficiency means work done per person per day, not the number of days a whole group takes. If a group of N people finishes one unit of work in D days, the team's combined person-days is N x D, and each individual's daily rate is 1 / (N x D). The smaller the value of N x D, the higher the individual efficiency.

Applying it to each group

  2. Boys: N x D = 6 x 12 = 72, so each boy's rate = 1/72 per day.

  3. Men: N x D = 9 x 9 = 81, so each man's rate = 1/81 per day.

  4. Women: N x D = 6 x 14 = 84, so each woman's rate = 1/84 per day.

Cross-check

Cross-check: compare the person-day totals 91, 72, 81 and 84. The smallest total is 72, which gives the largest individual daily rate 1/72. Hence one boy does more work per day than one girl, one man or one woman, so boys are the most efficient.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q98
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
subtopic: Efficiency Ratio and Comparative Work Rate
text: 6 men or 8 women can do a work in 25 days. The number of days required by 8 men and 6 women to complete the work is
solution:
When two groups can each finish the very same job in the very same number of days, their total daily outputs must be equal — this equality is what fixes the ratio between one individual's daily work in one group and one individual's daily work in the other group. That per-person efficiency ratio, combined with the job's total size, is what then decides how long any differently composed team needs for the same job.

  1. Let one man's one-day work be m and one woman's one-day work be w.

  2. Since 6 men finish the job in 25 days and 8 women finish the same job in 25 days, both groups produce the same total work: 6m × 25 = 8w × 25, so 6m = 8w, i.e. m : w = 4 : 3.

  3. Write the job as 24 units (the LCM of 6 and 8). Then 6 men completing 24 units in 25 days gives 1 man's daily work = 24 ÷ (6 × 25) = 4/25 unit; 8 women completing 24 units in 25 days gives 1 woman's daily work = 24 ÷ (8 × 25) = 3/25 unit — consistent with the 4 : 3 ratio.

  4. The new team of 8 men and 6 women therefore does 8 × 4/25 + 6 × 3/25 = 32/25 + 18/25 = 50/25 = 2 units per day.

  5. Days required = total work ÷ daily rate = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 days.

Cross-checking with the man-equivalent route: since 1 woman = 3/4 man (from the 4 : 3 ratio), 8 men and 6 women equal 8 + 6 × 3/4 = 12.5 man-equivalents. The whole job equals 6 men's 25-day output, i.e. 6 × 25 = 150 man-days. So the new team needs 150 ÷ 12.5 = 12 days — the same result.

So the work is completed in 12 days.

Taking a woman's daily efficiency as seven-sixths of a man's, 8 men and 6 women together equal 8 + (6 × 7/6) = 15 man-equivalents; against the 150 man-day total this works out to approximately 10 days.

Taking a woman's daily efficiency as one-and-a-half times a man's, 8 men and 6 women together equal 8 + (6 × 3/2) = 17 man-equivalents; against the 150 man-day total this works out to approximately 9 days.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q72

solution:
Concept: When a problem says that "A men OR B women can do a job in D days", it means each group ALONE completes the SAME job in D days, so their total effort in worker-days is equal: A × D man-days = B × D woman-days = one full job. This lets us find each individual's daily work rate, and then combine any mix of men and women using those rates.

Application:

  1. Total work in man-days: 3 men complete the wall in 43 days, so total work = 3 × 43 = 129 man-days.

  2. Total work in woman-days: 4 women complete the wall in 43 days, so total work = 4 × 43 = 172 woman-days.

  3. One man's daily rate = 1/129 of the wall, since 129 man-days make up 1 wall.

  4. One woman's daily rate = 1/172 of the wall, since 172 woman-days make up 1 wall.

  5. Combined daily rate of 7 men and 5 women = 7 × (1/129) + 5 × (1/172) = 7/129 + 5/172.

  6. Put both fractions over the LCM of 129 and 172, which is 516: 7/129 = 28/516 and 5/172 = 15/516.

  7. Add the fractions: 28/516 + 15/516 = 43/516 = 1/12 of the wall per day.

  8. At a combined rate of 1/12 of the wall per day, the whole wall is finished in 12 days.

Then 7 men and 5 women together equal 7 + 5 × (3/4) = 7 + 3.75 = 10.75 man-equivalents. Since 3 men finish the wall in 43 days, one man-equivalent's daily rate is 1/(3 × 43) = 1/129 of the wall, matching the rate found in step 3, so 10.75 man-equivalents' daily rate is 10.75/129 = 43/516 = 1/12 of the wall per day — the same rate found above, confirming the day count.

Result: 7 men and 5 women together complete the wall in 12 days.

title: IOCL Technical Attendant Numerical Ability 2024 Q77
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: हितेश अकेले एक कार्य को 11 दिनों में पूरा कर सकता है और जितेश उसी कार्य को अकेले 10 दिनों में पूरा कर सकता है। उन्होंने एक साथ कार्य करना शुरू किया, लेकिन हितेश को कार्य पूरा होने से 6 दिन पहले कार्य छोड़ना पड़ा। कार्य कितने दिनों में पूरा होगा?
solution:
अवधारणा

यदि कोई व्यक्ति किसी कार्य को a दिनों में पूरा करता है, तो उसकी एक दिन की कार्य-दर 1/a होती है। साथ काम करते समय दरें जुड़ती हैं; जो व्यक्ति पहले काम छोड़ता है, उसके कार्य-दिन कुल समय से अलग गिने जाते हैं।

कुल किए गए कार्य को 1 मानकर प्रत्येक व्यक्ति की दर × उसके वास्तविक कार्य-दिन लिखने से समय का समीकरण बनता है।

अनुप्रयोग

  1. मान लें कि कार्य पूरा होने में कुल t दिन लगे। जितेश ने t दिन और हितेश ने t − 6 दिन काम किया।

  2. दोनों का किया हुआ कार्य जोड़ने पर (t − 6)/11 + t/10 = 1।

  3. हर को 110 से गुणा करने पर 10(t − 6) + 11t = 110।

  4. अर्थात 10t − 60 + 11t = 110, इसलिए 21t = 170।

  5. अतः t = 170/21 = 8 2/21 दिन।

पुनः जाँच

  1. कुल कार्य 110 इकाई मानें। तब हितेश और जितेश की दरें क्रमशः 10 और 11 इकाई प्रतिदिन हैं।

  2. यदि दोनों x दिन साथ काम करें और जितेश अंतिम 6 दिन अकेले काम करे, तो 21x + 11 × 6 = 110।

  3. इससे x = 44/21 दिन और कुल समय x + 6 = 170/21 = 8 2/21 दिन मिलता है।

परिणाम

कार्य 8 2/21 दिनों में पूरा होगा।

title: An army post with men has provision of food for
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: An army post with 1800 men has provision of food for 50 days. After 10 days, some of the men go back to the base camp due to injuries. The remaining food is now enough for the next 50 days for the remaining men. What is the number of men who went back to the base camp?
solution:
Concept

In ration/provision problems, total food is measured in man-days: total man-days = (number of men) × (number of days the food lasts). This quantity is conserved — the man-days consumed plus the man-days still available always equal the original total, regardless of how the men or days change.

Application

  1. Original total food = 1800 men × 50 days = 90000 man-days.

  2. Food eaten in the first 10 days by all 1800 men = 1800 × 10 = 18000 man-days.

  3. Food left after 10 days = 90000 − 18000 = 72000 man-days.

  4. Let the number of remaining men be R. This leftover food must last the next 50 days, so R × 50 = 72000, giving R = 1440 men.

  5. Men who went back = original − remaining = 1800 − 1440 = 360.

Cross-check

Verify by the other route: the untouched 40 days of the original schedule hold 1800 × 40 = 72000 man-days, which matches the leftover food. Spread over 50 days that is 72000 ÷ 50 = 1440 men, so 360 men must have left — consistent with the man-days balance.

optionFeedback.html: A departure of 350 would leave a strength whose 50-day requirement does not match the food untouched after the first 10 days, so the man-day balance is not satisfied by this figure.
With 360 men returning, the strength that stays behind needs exactly the food left untouched after the first 10 days over the next 50 days, so the man-day balance closes for this figure.
A departure of 250 leaves too large a strength to be sustained by the food remaining after the first 10 days for a further 50 days, so the requirement exceeds the available man-days.
A departure of 310 also leaves a strength whose 50-day food requirement overshoots the man-days left after the first 10 days, so this figure does not balance the provisions either.

title: An army of men has provision for days. After days
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: An army of 2100 men has provision for 50 days. After 10 days due to injuries some of them left and the food were now enough for next 50 days for remaining men. The number of men left is:
solution:
Concept

In any provisions/work problem the total resource is conserved and equals the product men × days, measured in man-days. The same stock of food gives a fixed number of man-days; if the number of men changes, the days it lasts adjust so that men × days stays equal to the food that remains.

Application

  1. Total food provisioned at the start = 2100 × 50 = 105000 man-days.

  2. Food consumed in the first 10 days by all 2100 men = 2100 × 10 = 21000 man-days.

  3. Food still remaining after 10 days = 105000 − 21000 = 84000 man-days.

  4. Let the number of men remaining be R. This remaining food must last 50 more days: R × 50 = 84000.

  5. Solve for R: R = 84000 ÷ 50 = 1680 men remaining.

  6. Men who left = original men − remaining men = 2100 − 1680 = 420.

Cross-check

Put R = 1680 back in: 1680 men for 50 days need 1680 × 50 = 84000 man-days, which is exactly the food left after 10 days. The balance holds, so 420 men left.

optionFeedback.html: Reaching 400 typically follows from not reducing the original stock by what the whole force has already eaten during the first stretch of days, so the food base used in the final division is set incorrectly. Fix the provisions figure before splitting it over the new period.

420 is the departure count for which the men who stay consume precisely the provisions on hand across the extended period; the head-count and the days settle the resource exactly, with no surplus and no shortfall, which is what the balance requires.

410 comes from an error in the subtraction that converts the surviving strength into a departure count; the arithmetic of removing the leavers from the starting total has not been carried out cleanly, so the figure does not satisfy the resource equation.

650 generally results from mismanaging the days that have already passed — for example treating the entire original supply as untouched when setting up the equation — which distorts the relationship between people, days, and food and yields an off figure.

Concept

In provision problems the total stock of food is measured in man-days: total man-days = (number of men) x (number of days). This quantity is fixed by how much food exists, so the food eaten in any period equals (men present) x (days elapsed), and the food still left equals the original total minus what has been consumed.

  5. Men who left = original men - remaining men = 1500 - 1200 = 300.

Verify the balance: 1200 remaining men over 50 days need 1200 x 50 = 60000 man-days, exactly the food left after the first 10 days. So 300 is the number of men who left.

title: IOCL Junior Engineering Assistant - IV Numerical Ability 2024 Q78
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: 102 men have provisions for 12 days. If 34 men leave, for how many days will the same provisions last for the remaining men?
solution:
Concept

For a fixed quantity of provisions and an unchanged daily consumption rate per person, the number of people and the number of days vary inversely.

Therefore, people × days remains constant; this product is the total supply measured in man-days.

Application

  1. Calculate the available supply: 102 × 12 = 1,224 man-days.

  2. Calculate the remaining group: 102 − 34 = 68 men.

  3. Let the provisions last d days. Then 68d = 1,224, so d = 1,224 ÷ 68 = 18 days.

Cross-check

At 68 men for 18 days, consumption is 68 × 18 = 1,224 man-days, exactly the original supply.

Hence, the provisions will last 18 days.

For 18 days, 68 men would require 68 × 18 = 1,224 man-days of provisions.
For 16 days, 68 men would require 68 × 16 = 1,088 man-days of provisions.
For 22 days, 68 men would require 68 × 22 = 1,496 man-days of provisions.

title: Men can do work in days working hours day. If
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: 10 men can do a work in 15 days working 4 hours a day. If after 5 days, 4 men leave the work, then remaining work can be done in how many days?
solution:
Total work: 10 men * 15 days * 4 hours/day = 600 man-hours.

Work done in 5 days: 10 men * 5 days * 4 hours/day = 200 man-hours.

Remaining work: 600 - 200 = 400 man-hours.

Remaining men: 10 - 4 = 6 men.

Calculate remaining days (D): 6 men * D * 4 hours/day = 400 man-hours.

24 * D = 400

D = 400 / 24 = 50 / 3 days.

Final Answer: Option 1 (50/3)

text: The water from one outlet, flowing at a constant rate, can fill the swimming pool in 9 hours. The water from second outlet, flowing at a constant rate can fill up the same pool in approximately in 5 hours. If both the outlets are used at the same time, approximately what is the number of hours required to fill the pool?
solution:
Assume tank capacity is 45 Liters.

Given that the first pipe fills the tank in 9 hours.

So its capacity is 45 / 9 = 5 Liters/ Hour.

Second pipe fills the tank in 5 hours.

So its capacity is 45 / 5 = 9 Liters/Hour. If both pipes are opened together, then combined capacity is 14 liters/hour.

To fill a tank of capacity 45 liters, Both pipes takes 45 / 14 = 3.21 Hours.

title: There are four mixtures and containing liquids and in different
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: There are four mixtures (P, Q, R and S) containing liquids X and Y in different proportions. Mixture P contains X and Y in the ratio 1:2, Q in the ratio 11:13, R in the ratio 5:3 and S in the ratio 19:5. Which of the following parts, mixed in equal quantity will have the highest concentration?
solution:
Step 1: Find the fraction of X in each mixture:

  • P: X/(X+Y) = 1/(1+2) = 1/3 = 8/24

  • Q: 11/(11+13) = 11/24

  • R: 5/(5+3) = 5/8 = 15/24

  • S: 19/(19+5) = 19/24

Step 2: When equal quantities of two mixtures are mixed, the resulting fraction of X is the average of their fractions.

  • Q and R: (11/24 + 15/24)/2 = 26/48 = 13/24 ≈ 0.5417

  • P and R: (8/24 + 15/24)/2 = 23/48 ≈ 0.4792

  • P and S: (8/24 + 19/24)/2 = 27/48 = 9/16 = 0.5625

  • Q and P: (11/24 + 8/24)/2 = 19/48 ≈ 0.3958

When a mixture's ratio changes because only one ingredient is added, the quantity of the untouched ingredient stays fixed. Express both the original and target ratios in terms of that fixed quantity, then find how much of the added ingredient is needed to reach the new ratio.

title: To earn an extra profit, shopkeeper mixes kg of rice
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: To earn an extra profit, a shopkeeper mixes 30 kg of rice purchased at Rs 36/kg with 26 kg of rice purchased at Rs 20/kg. What percentage of profit will he make if he sells the mixture at Rs 30/kg?
solution:
Concept: When two quantities of goods with different cost prices are mixed, the cost price of the mixture is the quantity-weighted average of the individual cost prices — the total cost of both lots divided by the total quantity. The profit percentage on the mixture is then found in the usual way: (Selling Price − Cost Price) ÷ Cost Price × 100, using this weighted cost price as the base.

Applying this to the given mixture:

  1. Total cost of the mixture = (30 kg × ₹36/kg) + (26 kg × ₹20/kg) = ₹1080 + ₹520 = ₹1600.

  2. Total quantity of the mixture = 30 kg + 26 kg = 56 kg.

  3. Cost price of the mixture per kg = ₹1600 ÷ 56 = ₹200/7 ≈ ₹28.57 per kg.

  4. Selling price per kg = ₹30.

  5. Profit per kg = ₹30 − ₹200/7 = ₹10/7.

  6. Profit percentage = (Profit ÷ Cost Price) × 100 = [(10/7) ÷ (200/7)] × 100 = (10 ÷ 200) × 100 = 5%.

Cross-check: Working with totals instead of per-kg values gives the same result — total revenue from selling all 56 kg at ₹30/kg is 56 × 30 = ₹1680, so the total profit is ₹1680 − ₹1600 = ₹80, and the profit percentage is (80 ÷ 1600) × 100 = 5%, confirming the answer.

Hence, the shopkeeper makes a profit of 5%.

optionFeedback.html: This figure comes from misreading the 26 kg lot as 20 kg while totalling the mixture (a natural slip, since 20 also appears elsewhere in the question as a rate). On that mistaken 50 kg total, the deal actually works out to a small loss whose size is close to this figure — treating that loss magnitude as a profit percentage, through a sign slip, lands close to this option.

The mixture's overall cost price works out to ₹200/7 per kg (≈₹28.57/kg) once the 30 kg and 26 kg lots are combined by their actual quantities. Selling at ₹30/kg gives a profit of ₹10/7 per kg, which is exactly 5% of the cost price of the mixture.

This figure comes from taking the mixture's cost price as the plain, unweighted average of ₹36/kg and ₹20/kg — that is, ignoring that 30 kg and 26 kg were mixed in different amounts — which pushes the resulting profit percentage up close to this figure instead of the correctly weighted one.

This figure comes from working the profit out as a percentage of the selling price (₹30/kg) instead of the cost price of the mixture; that understated base brings the resulting percentage down close to this figure rather than the correct one.

text: In a chemistry lab two beakers A and B contains 36% and 40% of spirit respectively. If two liters from A is mixed with 4 liters of B. The ratio of spirit and water in the resulting mixture is:
solution:
Concept

When two liquid solutions are blended, the amount of any component in the mixture is the sum of that component's amount in each part, where component amount = volume × its fractional concentration. The remaining volume is the other component. Once you have the component totals, the required ratio is just one total to the other.

Application

  1. Spirit drawn from A = 2 × 36% = 2 × 0.36 = 0.72 litre.

  2. Spirit drawn from B = 4 × 40% = 4 × 0.40 = 1.60 litre.

  3. Total spirit = 0.72 + 1.60 = 2.32 litre.

  4. Total mixture poured = 2 + 4 = 6 litre.

  5. Water = total − spirit = 6 − 2.32 = 3.68 litre.

  6. Spirit : Water = 2.32 : 3.68. Multiply both by 100 to clear decimals → 232 : 368, then divide by their HCF 8 → 29 : 46.

Cross-check

Scale the answer back: 29 + 46 = 75 parts represent 6 litre, so 1 part = 0.08 litre. Spirit = 29 × 0.08 = 2.32 litre and water = 46 × 0.08 = 3.68 litre, which matches the totals computed above. Hence the ratio of spirit to water is 29 : 46.

title: Jeweler mixed gold and copper in two proportions. In type
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: A jeweler mixed gold and copper in two proportions. In type A alloy, 6 gm gold is mixed with 5 gm copper and in type B alloy, 5 gm gold is mixed with 3 gm copper. If the jeweler mixed 122 gm gold and 90 gm copper, then find the weight of type B alloy.
solution:
Concept

In a fixed-ratio mixture (alloy), each constituent is a fixed fraction of every batch. If you mix a quantity of one alloy and a quantity of another, the total of each constituent is the sum of its contributions from both alloys. So two unknown alloy quantities can be found by writing one linear equation per constituent and solving the simultaneous pair.

Application

  1. Type A is gold:copper = 6:5, so one A-batch = 6 + 5 = 11 gm. Type B is gold:copper = 5:3, so one B-batch = 5 + 3 = 8 gm. Let a = number of A-batches and b = number of B-batches.

  2. Gold equation (total gold = 122): 6a + 5b = 122.

  3. Copper equation (total copper = 90): 5a + 3b = 90.

  4. Eliminate b: multiply the gold equation by 3 and the copper equation by 5 to get 18a + 15b = 366 and 25a + 15b = 450. Subtract: 7a = 84, so a = 12.

  5. Substitute a = 12 into 5a + 3b = 90: 60 + 3b = 90, so 3b = 30 and b = 10.

  6. Weight of type B alloy = b x 8 = 10 x 8 = 80 gm.

Cross-check

Weight of type A alloy = a x 11 = 12 x 11 = 132 gm. Total alloy = 132 + 80 = 212 gm, which equals total gold + total copper = 122 + 90 = 212 gm. Gold used = 6(12) + 5(10) = 72 + 50 = 122 and copper used = 5(12) + 3(10) = 60 + 30 = 90, matching the given amounts exactly.

Therefore the weight of type B alloy is 80 gm.

optionFeedback.html: This total arises from setting up one balance equation for gold and one for copper, solving them together for the whole-number batch counts, and reading off the type-B amount from its batch count.
This total mistakenly carries over type A's per-batch gold figure (6 gm) as if it were the type-B batch weight, instead of computing type B's own batch weight from its stated gold-and-copper mix.

This total arises from carrying an arithmetic slip into the elimination step, for example mis-multiplying one of the two balance equations before subtracting, which changes the solved batch count for type B and produces this smaller total.

title: Rice mixture ratio for 15% gain
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: In what ratio should rice costing Rs. 90 per kg be mixed with rice costing Rs. 63 per kg so that selling the mixture at Rs. 86.25 per kg gives a gain of 15%?
solution:
CONCEPT

When a mixture is sold at a gain, first remove the gain from the selling price to find the cost price of the mixture. In alligation, the ratio of the dearer item to the cheaper item equals the opposite differences from the required mean cost.

APPLICATION

  1. Selling price of the mixture = Rs. 86.25 per kg and gain = 15%.

  2. Cost price of the mixture = 86.25 / 1.15 = Rs. 75 per kg.

  3. Dearer rice costs Rs. 90 per kg and cheaper rice costs Rs. 63 per kg, so the required mean cost Rs. 75 lies between them.

  4. By alligation, dearer : cheaper = (75 - 63) : (90 - 75) = 12 : 15 = 4 : 5.

CROSS-CHECK

Using 4 : 5, the weighted cost is (4 × 90 + 5 × 63) / 9 = (360 + 315) / 9 = Rs. 75 per kg. Adding 15% gives 75 × 1.15 = Rs. 86.25, matching the given selling price.

CONTRAST

  • 5 : 4 gives a higher weighted cost because it puts more quantity on the costlier rice.

  • 3 : 5 gives a lower weighted cost because it puts too little quantity on the costlier rice for this target mean.

  • 2 : 3 also keeps the weighted cost below the required mean for the stated selling-price condition.

RESULT

The required ratio of Rs. 90 rice to Rs. 63 rice is 4 : 5.

optionFeedback.html: The ratio 5 : 4 puts too much weight on the costlier rice, so the mixture cost rises above the target cost obtained after removing the gain.
The ratio 4 : 5 balances the two costs around the target mixture cost, so the selling price condition with 15% gain is satisfied.
The ratio 3 : 5 gives too little weight to the costlier rice, making the mixture cost fall below the target cost implied by the selling price.
The ratio 2 : 3 also underweights the costlier rice, so the resulting mixture cost does not reach the required mean cost.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q65
subject: Mathematics and Aptitude
text: In what ratio should tea costing ₹62 per kg be mixed with tea costing ₹72 per kg so that the mixture costs ₹64.50 per kg?
solution:
Concept

When two ingredients with different unit prices are mixed to obtain an intermediate price, the alligation rule compares each ingredient's distance from the mean price.

The quantity ratio of the cheaper ingredient to the dearer ingredient is (dearer price − mean price) : (mean price − cheaper price).

Application

  1. Let the required quantities of the ₹62 tea and the ₹72 tea be x kg and y kg respectively.

  2. By the weighted-average equation, 62x + 72y = 64.50(x + y).

  3. Rearranging gives 64.50x − 62x = 72y − 64.50y, so 2.50x = 7.50y.

  4. Therefore x : y = 7.50 : 2.50 = 3 : 1.

Cross-check

Using three equal parts of ₹62 tea and one equal part of ₹72 tea gives (3 × 62 + 1 × 72) ÷ 4 = 258 ÷ 4 = ₹64.50 per kg.

Hence, the tea costing ₹62 per kg and the tea costing ₹72 per kg should be mixed in the ratio 3 : 1.

For the ratio 4 : 3, the weighted price is (4 × ₹62 + 3 × ₹72) ÷ 7 = ₹66.29 per kg (approximately).
For the ratio 5 : 3, the weighted price is (5 × ₹62 + 3 × ₹72) ÷ 8 = ₹65.75 per kg.
